# Habit Forever — full text

Habit Forever is a habit tracker for iPhone and iPad (iOS 17 or later) by independent developer Mohamed Elatabany. Track check-off or number habits with goals, reminders, notes, streaks and colorful day-by-day grids, plus Home Screen and Lock Screen widgets and Siri Shortcuts. There is no account, and habit data stays on your device. It is free for up to three habits; Habit Forever Pro (yearly, monthly or a one-time lifetime purchase) adds unlimited habits, deeper insights, widgets for every habit and backup export/import. It is rated 4.6★ on the App Store, from 17 ratings worldwide, where it is listed as “Habit Forever: Streak Tracker” (formerly “Habit Streak Tracker: Routines”).

---

# Habit Forever
URL: https://habitforever.app/
Updated: 2026-11-18



Play
 
 
 Read · 12 weeks

 
 
 
 
 The habit tracker for iPhone and iPad

 Small habits, every day, in color.
 Check in with one tap and every day you show up becomes a colored square. Count glasses or pages, set reminders, and watch your year fill in.

 
 
 
 
 ★★★★★ 4.6 on the App Store · from 17 ratings

 Free for up to three habits. No account, no ads.

 
 
 On a computer? Point your iPhone camera here to open Habit Forever in the App Store.

 
 
 

 
 
 

## How it works

 Three steps, then it fits into your day. The whole thing takes seconds.

 
 
 
- 

### Pick a small habit
Type a name or start from an idea. Choose every day or the days that suit you, and add a reminder if you like.

 
- 

### Check in
Tap once when it’s done. For number habits, log the amount: glasses of water, pages, minutes, kilometers or your own unit.

 
- 

### Watch it fill with color
Every day you show up becomes a square. Streaks, your best run and your consistency are worked out for you.

 

 

 
 
 

## Everything a habit needs, nothing it doesn’t

 
 
 
 
 

### More than a checkmark

 Some habits are a yes or no. Others are a number. Habit Forever handles both.

 
 
- Reach a number (8 glasses, 20 pages), or stay under a limit for things you want less of
 
- Goals for each day or each week, on every day, weekdays or the days you choose
 
- Add a note to any check-in, and fill in a missed day from the last seven days
 

 
 
 
 
 
 

### See what’s working

 Your current streak, your best streak and how consistent you’ve been. Each habit gets its own grid of days, like a contribution graph for your life.

 
 
- Progress across all your habits at a glance, and celebrations when a streak hits a milestone
 
- Pro adds deeper patterns: your best days, time of day and month by month
 

 
 
 
 
 
 

### Your day, your way

 See every habit on one screen in the layout you like, then keep them close with widgets and Siri.

 
 
- Three layouts: Grid, Board (months of days per habit) and Week
 
- Home Screen and Lock Screen widgets that let you check in without opening the app
 
- Siri and Shortcuts: check in (with an amount and a note), hear your streak, open a habit
 
- Reminders that stay quiet on days you’ve already checked in
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

## Your habits stay on your iPhone

 There’s no account to create and nothing to sign in to. Your habits, check-ins and notes are stored on your device. With Pro you can export a backup file whenever you want, and import it on another device. Purchases are handled by Apple and RevenueCat. Read the privacy policy.

 
 

 
 
 

## Free to start. Pro when you want more.

 Prices are shown in the app before you buy, in your currency.

 
 
 
 

### Free

 
 
- Up to three habits
 
- Check-off and number habits, goals and limits
 
- Reminders, notes, streaks and day grids
 
- A widget for your first habit
 

 
 
 

### Habit Forever Pro

 
 
- Unlimited habits
 
- Deeper insights and patterns
 
- Widgets for every habit
 
- Backup export and import
 

 Yearly, monthly, or pay once with Lifetime and keep it for good.

## Questions

 Is Habit Forever free?
Yes. Habit Forever is free to download and free for up to three habits, with check-ins, number goals, reminders, notes, streaks and day grids. Habit Forever Pro is optional and adds unlimited habits, deeper insights, widgets for every habit and backup export and import, as a yearly or monthly subscription or a one-time lifetime purchase.

 Do I need an account?
No. There is no account or sign-in. Your habits, check-ins and notes are stored on your device.

 Does Habit Forever sync with iCloud?
No. Habit data stays on the device. With Pro you can export a backup file and import it on another iPhone or iPad.

 Can I track numbers, not just yes or no?
Yes. A habit can be a simple check-off or a number such as glasses, pages, minutes, distance, spending or a unit you name, with a number to reach or a limit to stay under, per day or per week.

 Which devices does it run on?
Habit Forever runs on iPhone and iPad with iOS 17 or later. There is no Apple Watch, Mac or Android version.

 Is Habit Forever the app formerly called Habit Tracker?
Yes. The app was previously listed on the App Store as “Habit Streak Tracker: Routines” and showed “Habit Tracker” on the Home Screen. From version 4.0 it is called Habit Forever. It is the same app, and your habits and history carry over.

# About Habit Forever
URL: https://habitforever.app/about.html
Updated: 2026-10-22

Habit Forever is a small, independent app. One person designs it, builds it, answers the support email and writes the guides on this site.

## Who makes it

I’m Mohamed Elatabany, an independent iOS developer. I build Habit Forever in Swift and SwiftUI and publish it on the App Store under my own name. There’s no company, investor or ad network behind it: the app is paid for by people who choose Habit Forever Pro.

I started it because I wanted a habit tracker that shows the shape of my days, not just a number. Every day you show up becomes a colored square, and over weeks those squares tell you more than any streak counter.

## What the app stands for

 
- Small and quick. Checking in should take a second. Adding a habit should take less than a minute.
 
- Your data is yours. No account and no sign-in. Habits and notes are stored on your device, and Pro lets you export a backup file whenever you like.
 
- Free that’s actually useful. Up to three habits with goals, reminders, notes, streaks and grids, with no time limit.
 
- No ads. Not in the free version, not ever.

## How the guides are written

Every guide is written by me. Claims about Habit Forever come from the app itself, and I update them when the app changes. Claims about iOS follow Apple’s own documentation. Research is cited with links to the original papers, not to summaries. When I compare apps, I disclose that I make Habit Forever and I say when another app is the better fit. Each page shows when it was last updated.

If something is wrong or out of date, email me at atabany.apps@gmail.com and I’ll correct it.

## About the name

Until version 4.0 the app was listed on the App Store as “Habit Streak Tracker: Routines” and showed “Habit Tracker” on the Home Screen. It’s now Habit Forever, listed as “Habit Forever: Streak Tracker”. Same app, same developer, and your data carries over.

 

 

## About Habit Forever

 Habit Forever is a habit tracker for iPhone and iPad (iOS 17 or later) by independent developer Mohamed Elatabany. Track check-off or number habits with goals, reminders, notes, streaks and colorful day-by-day grids, plus Home Screen and Lock Screen widgets and Siri Shortcuts. There is no account, and habit data stays on your device. It is free for up to three habits; Habit Forever Pro (yearly, monthly or a one-time lifetime purchase) adds unlimited habits, deeper insights, widgets for every habit and backup export/import. It is rated 4.6★ on the App Store, from 17 ratings worldwide, where it is listed as “Habit Forever: Streak Tracker” (formerly “Habit Streak Tracker: Routines”).

# The best habit tracker apps for iPhone in 2026
URL: https://habitforever.app/compare/best-habit-tracker-apps-iphone.html
Updated: 2026-11-18

There is no single best habit tracker. Streaks suits Apple Watch and Health users, HabitKit and Habit Forever suit people who love a visual grid without an account, Habitify suits people on several platforms, and Habitica suits people who want a game.

Disclosure: we make Habit Forever, one of the apps on this list. We have tried to describe every app fairly, including where others are the better choice, and we only state facts we could check from each app's own listing or website. Features and prices change, so confirm details on the App Store before you buy.

The right habit tracker depends on what you need most: Apple Watch support, syncing across devices, a game, or a private app with no account. The table below gives the short version.

## Comparison at a glance

 | | App | Pricing model | Account needed | Standout | Best for

 | Streaks | Paid upfront, no in-app purchases | No (iCloud sync) | Apple Design Award; Apple Health auto-complete; Apple Watch | Apple Watch and Health users

 | HabitKit | Free + Pro (monthly, yearly or lifetime) | No (on device) | Grid layouts; yes/no, count and amount habits | Visual, private tracking

 | Habitify | Free + subscription or lifetime | Yes (Sign in with Apple), cloud sync | iOS, Android, Mac and web; Zapier and IFTTT | People on several platforms

 | (Not Boring) Habits | Subscription, limited free use | — | Apple Design Award; design-led 3D look | People who want something delightful

 | Way of Life | Free with in-app purchases | — | Done, not done or skip for each day | Simple yes/no journaling

 | Habitica | — | Yes | Gamified role-playing game; open source; parties | People motivated by games and friends

 | Everyday | Subscription + lifetime | Yes (account and web sync) | Colorful calendar view | A bright month-at-a-glance view

 | Strides | Free with in-app purchases | — | Habits and goals; habit, target, average and milestone trackers | Mixing habits with bigger goals

 | Habit Forever | Free for 3 habits + Pro (yearly, monthly or lifetime) | No (on device) | Number goals to reach or stay under, per day or week; contribution grids; widgets; Siri | Number habits and limits, privately

"—" means we could not confirm the detail. Check the app's App Store page.

## How to choose

- Do you wear an Apple Watch or want Health data to tick habits off? Streaks is the strongest choice here.

- Do you use Android, a Mac or the web too? Habitify works across all of them, with an account.

- Do you want no account at all? Streaks, HabitKit and Habit Forever all work without one.

- Do you track numbers, not just done or not done? HabitKit, Strides and Habit Forever all handle amounts.

- Does a game keep you going? Habitica turns habits into a role-playing game.

## Streaks

Streaks, by Crunchy Bagel, is a long-standing favorite and an Apple Design Award winner. You pay once upfront, with no in-app purchases. It needs no account and syncs through iCloud. Habits can be completed automatically from Apple Health data, and it has an Apple Watch app. Its App Store listing describes tracking up to 24 tasks.

Choose it if you live in Apple's ecosystem and want habits like steps or workouts to complete themselves. See our Streaks alternative page for a closer comparison.

## HabitKit

HabitKit, by Sebastian Roehl, is known for its grid layouts, where each habit fills in a tile pattern over time. It runs without an account, with data on the device, and supports yes/no, count and amount habits. It is free with a Pro upgrade available monthly, yearly or as a lifetime purchase.

Choose it if you want a clean, visual tracker. It is the closest app to Habit Forever; see our HabitKit alternative page.

## Habitify

Habitify runs on iOS, Android, Mac and the web, with an account (including Sign in with Apple) and cloud sync. It groups habits into areas and connects to Zapier and IFTTT. It is free with a subscription or lifetime upgrade.

Choose it if you switch between devices that are not all Apple, or want automations. For a closer look, see our Habitify alternative page.

## (Not Boring) Habits

(Not Boring) Habits is a design-led tracker with a playful 3D style and an Apple Design Award. It is subscription-based with limited free use.

Choose it if how an app feels matters as much as what it does.

## Way of Life

Way of Life keeps things simple: each day you mark a habit done, not done, or skipped. It is free with in-app purchases.

Choose it if you want quick yes/no logging and do not care about counting.

## Habitica

Habitica turns your habits into a role-playing game: you level up a character and can join parties with friends. It is open source and requires an account.

Choose it if plain checklists bore you and social accountability helps.

## Everyday

Everyday shows habits on a colorful calendar. It uses an account with web sync and offers a subscription or a lifetime purchase.

Choose it if you want a bright monthly calendar view and web access.

## Strides

Strides combines habits with longer goals and offers four tracker types: habit, target, average and milestone. It is free with in-app purchases.

Choose it if you want to track a savings goal or a weight target next to daily habits.

 

## Habit Forever

Habit Forever is our app, for iPhone and iPad on iOS 17 or later. It tracks check-off habits or number habits such as pages, glasses, minutes, distance or spending. Goals can be a number to reach or a limit to stay under for habits you want less of, per day or per week, on every day, weekdays or chosen days. Each habit has a current and best streak, a consistency figure, and a colorful day-by-day contribution grid. You can check in from Home Screen and Lock Screen widgets, or with Siri and Shortcuts.

There is no account, and habit data stays on your device. It is free for up to three habits; Habit Forever Pro (yearly, monthly or a one-time lifetime purchase) adds unlimited habits, deeper insights, widgets for every habit and JSON backup export and import. It is rated 4.6★ on the App Store, from 17 ratings, so it is still a young app.

Where others are better: Habit Forever has no Apple Watch app, no Apple Health integration, no iCloud sync, no Android or web version, and no social features. If you need any of those, Streaks, Habitify or Habitica will serve you better.

Choose it if you track numbers and limits, want weekly targets, and prefer no account.

## Also worth knowing

Loop Habit Tracker is a popular free, open-source tracker, but it is Android only. If you are coming from Loop, read Loop Habit Tracker for iPhone. If you would rather not use an app at all, see how to track habits on iPhone with built-in apps, or print our printable habit tracker. If you want to avoid a subscription, read habit trackers without a subscription.

## FAQ

What is the best habit tracker app for iPhone?
It depends on your needs: Streaks suits Apple Watch and Health users, Habitify suits people on several platforms, Habitica suits people who like games, and HabitKit and Habit Forever suit people who want a visual grid without an account.

Which habit tracker works with Apple Watch?
Streaks has an Apple Watch app and can complete habits automatically from Apple Health data, while Habit Forever does not have an Apple Watch app.

Which habit trackers do not need an account?
Streaks, HabitKit and Habit Forever all work without creating an account.

Is there a free habit tracker for iPhone?
Several apps have free tiers, including HabitKit, Habitify, Way of Life, Strides and Habit Forever, which is free for up to three habits.

Which habit tracker is a one-time purchase?
Streaks is paid upfront with no in-app purchases, and HabitKit, Habitify, Everyday and Habit Forever offer a lifetime option alongside their subscriptions.

# Looking for a Habitify alternative?
URL: https://habitforever.app/compare/habitify-alternative.html
Updated: 2026-11-18

Habitify is the better choice if you need Android, Mac, web or Apple Watch, sync across devices, or integrations such as Apple Health and Zapier. Habit Forever may suit you better if you only use iPhone or iPad and want no account at all, data kept on your device, limits for habits you want less of, and a one-time lifetime option.

Disclosure: I make Habit Forever. Habitify is a well-established app that does many things Habit Forever does not, so this page tries to be straight about both sides. I checked Habitify's details on its website, pricing page and App Store listing on 18 November 2026; where I could not confirm something, the table says "—". Plans and features change, so check Habitify's own pages before deciding.

## What Habitify does well

Habitify, by Unstatic Ltd Co, is one of the most complete habit trackers available.

- Every platform. Its App Store listing covers iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch and Apple Vision, and its website adds Android and a web app.

- Sync. Your habits sync across devices through your account, including Sign in with Apple.

- Integrations. The App Store listing says it can log progress automatically from Apple Health, Google Health/Fit, Fitbit, Strava and Screen Time or RescueTime, with your consent. Its pricing page lists Apple and Google calendar integrations, an API, and automation through Zapier and IFTTT on its paid plan.

- A full toolkit. Time-of-day sections for your routine, a built-in timer, notes, mood tracking, challenges with friends, Siri support, and reminders that can follow a habit stack or a location.

- Languages. The App Store lists English and 39 other languages.

On pricing, Habitify's pricing page shows a free plan (listed at 3 habits, with cross-platform sync) and a Premium plan billed annually or once as a lifetime purchase. The App Store listing shows Free, Plus and Pro tiers with monthly, yearly, lifetime and family purchases, and a recent release note says free users can now create more habits, with those beyond the basic limit view-only. The two sources describe the plans differently, so check in the app for what applies to you.

## When Habitify is the better choice

- You use Android, a Mac, the web or an Apple Watch, or switch between devices. Habit Forever runs only on iPhone and iPad and has no sync.

- You want habits to complete themselves from Apple Health, Fitbit, Strava or Screen Time.

- You want Zapier, IFTTT, calendar integration or an API.

- You want a timer, mood tracking or challenges with friends inside your habit tracker.

- You need the app in a language other than English. Habit Forever is in English only.

If any of those matter, stay with Habitify. There is no point switching for a smaller feature set.

## Why some people look for an alternative

Common reasons are about simplicity and ownership: not wanting an account for a personal checklist, preferring data on the phone rather than a server, wanting to pay once rather than subscribe, or wanting fewer features and a calmer screen. Those are the areas where Habit Forever is different.

## Habitify and Habit Forever side by side

 | | | Habitify | Habit Forever

 | Platforms | iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch, Apple Vision, Android, web | iPhone and iPad (iOS 17 or later)

 | Account | Used for sync (Sign in with Apple available) | None

 | Where data lives | Synced across your devices | On your device only (no iCloud sync)

 | Apple Health and other integrations | Yes (Apple Health, Fitbit, Strava, Screen Time and more) | No

 | Zapier, IFTTT, API | Yes | No

 | Number habits | — | Yes, in any unit (pages, glasses, minutes, spending)

 | Maximum goals (limits) | — | Yes, for habits you want less of

 | Weekly goals | — | Yes, with streaks counted in weeks

 | Day-by-day history grid | Yearly completion view | A colorful grid for each habit

 | Siri | Yes | Yes: "Check In Habit" with optional amount and note, "Get Habit Streak", "Open Habit"

 | Home Screen and Lock Screen widgets with check-in | — | Yes

 | Timer, mood, challenges | Yes | No

 | Languages | English and 39 others | English

 | Free plan | Yes (see above) | Up to 3 habits, no time limit

 | Paid options | Subscriptions and lifetime | Yearly, monthly or a one-time lifetime purchase

 

## Where Habit Forever fits

Habit Forever is a habit tracker for iPhone and iPad that I build on my own. It does fewer things than Habitify on purpose.

### No account, on your device

You open it and start. There is no sign-up, and habit records and notes are stored on your device. The trade-off is real: there is no sync, so it is a poor fit if you track on several devices. For more on that trade-off, read how to choose a private habit tracker with no account.

### Numbers, limits and weekly goals

A habit can be a simple check-off or a number in any unit. Goals can be a minimum ("at least 20 pages"), or a maximum for habits you want less of ("at most 2 cups of coffee"), per day or per week. A weekly goal counts its streak in weeks. See weekly habit goals and how to track a habit you want to do less.

### Siri, Shortcuts and widgets

"Check in on Habit Forever" works with Siri as soon as the app is installed, and the Check In Habit action in Shortcuts takes an optional amount and note, so you can log from the Action button or an automation. See how to log habits with Siri and Shortcuts. Home Screen and Lock Screen widgets let you check in without opening the app.

### Free, or pay once

It is free for up to three habits with no time limit. Habit Forever Pro adds unlimited habits, deeper insights such as your strongest days and time of day, widgets for every habit, and JSON backup export and import, as a yearly or monthly plan or a one-time lifetime purchase. More in habit trackers without a subscription. It is rated 4.6★ on the App Store, from 17 ratings.

## If you switch

Habit Forever cannot import Habitify data; its import only reads its own backups. The simplest path is to start your main habits fresh and keep Habitify's history for reference. If you have years of history and use more than one device, that is a good reason to stay.

## More comparisons

See all nine apps in our best habit tracker apps for iPhone comparison. If you want an Apple Watch app without an account, read the Streaks alternative page; for a visual grid tracker, see the HabitKit alternative page.

## FAQ

What is a good alternative to Habitify?
If you only use iPhone or iPad, Habit Forever is an alternative with no account, data on your device, limits and weekly goals, and a one-time lifetime option; if you need Android, Mac, web or sync, Habitify remains the better fit.

Does Habitify work on Android and Mac?
Yes, Habitify's website lists iOS, Android and a web app, and its App Store listing covers iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch and Apple Vision.

Does Habit Forever need an account like Habitify?
No, Habit Forever works without an account and keeps your habit data on your device, with no sync between devices.

Can I import my Habitify data into Habit Forever?
No, Habit Forever cannot import Habitify data and only imports its own backups.

Does Habitify have a lifetime option?
Yes, Habitify's pricing page and App Store listing both show a lifetime purchase alongside its other plans.

## Sources

- Habit Forever on the App Store

# Looking for a HabitKit alternative?
URL: https://habitforever.app/compare/habitkit-alternative.html
Updated: 2026-11-18

HabitKit and Habit Forever are close: both show habits as colorful grids, need no account and keep data on your device. Habit Forever may suit you better if you want limits for habits you want less of, weekly goals, or Siri check-ins with an amount.

Disclosure: we make Habit Forever. HabitKit is the app most similar to ours, and a good one, so this page tries to be straight about where they match, where they differ, and what we could not verify.

If you like HabitKit's look but something is missing, the differences below are what to check. If HabitKit already does everything you need, there is little reason to switch.

## What HabitKit does well

HabitKit, by Sebastian Roehl, is a well-known visual habit tracker for iPhone.

- Grid layouts. Each habit fills in a tile grid over time, so a year of effort fits on one screen.

- No account, on device. You start tracking immediately and your data stays on your phone.

- Several habit types. It supports yes/no habits, count habits and amount habits.

- Flexible pricing. It is free, with a Pro upgrade available monthly, yearly or as a lifetime purchase.

For many people that is exactly right.

## What HabitKit and Habit Forever share

- A colorful grid of each habit's history, in the style of a GitHub contribution graph.

- No account and on-device storage.

- Number habits as well as simple check-offs.

- A free tier and a Pro upgrade with monthly, yearly and lifetime options.

So this is not a choice between a good app and a bad one. It comes down to details.

## Where Habit Forever is different

These are features we can confirm in Habit Forever. Where we could not verify the HabitKit side, the table says "—".

 | | | HabitKit | Habit Forever

 | Account needed | No | No

 | Data storage | On device | On device (no iCloud sync)

 | History grid | Yes, grid layouts | Yes, a day-by-day grid per habit

 | Yes/no and number habits | Yes (yes/no, count, amount) | Yes (check-off or number, with your own unit)

 | Maximum goals (limits) | — | Yes, for habits you want less of

 | Weekly goals (streak counts weeks) | — | Yes, plus daily

 | Siri and Shortcuts | — | "Check In Habit" with optional amount and note, "Get Habit Streak", "Open Habit"

 | Lock Screen widgets with check-in | — | Yes

 | Free tier | Yes | Up to 3 habits

 | Pro plans | Monthly, yearly, lifetime | Yearly, monthly, lifetime

### Limits for habits you want less of

Many habits are about doing less: screen time, coffee, spending. In Habit Forever a number habit can have a number to reach or a limit to stay under, so "at most 2 hours" counts as a success when you stay under it. See how to track a habit you want to do less.

### Weekly goals

Some habits do not fit a daily rhythm, such as the gym three times a week or two long walks. Habit Forever lets a habit have a weekly goal, and its streak counts weeks, so a rest day is not a miss. See weekly habit goals.

### Siri with amounts

The "Check In Habit" action works with Siri and Shortcuts and accepts an optional amount and note, so you can log "3 glasses" or "25 minutes" by voice or from an automation.

 

## Habit Forever in brief

Habit Forever is a habit tracker for iPhone and iPad (iOS 17 or later) by an independent developer. It tracks check-off or number habits with goals, reminders, notes, streaks and colorful day-by-day grids, plus Home Screen and Lock Screen widgets and Siri Shortcuts. Each habit shows its current and best streak and consistency, and you can fill in a past day you actually did or archive a habit and keep its history.

There is no account, and habit data stays on your device. It is free for up to three habits; Habit Forever Pro (yearly, monthly or a one-time lifetime purchase) adds unlimited habits, deeper insights such as your best days and time of day, widgets for every habit, and JSON backup export and import. It is rated 4.6★ on the App Store, from 17 ratings.

## When to stay with HabitKit

- You are happy with its grids and habit types and do not need limits or weekly goals.

- You have years of history in it and do not want to start again. Habit Forever cannot import HabitKit data; its import only reads its own JSON backups.

- You prefer its design. With two apps this close, taste is a perfectly good reason.

Habit Forever also has no iCloud sync, no Apple Watch app and no Apple Health integration. If those matter, read our Streaks alternative page.

## More comparisons

See all nine apps in our best habit tracker apps for iPhone comparison, our Habitify alternative page, or, if you came from Android, Loop Habit Tracker for iPhone. For privacy questions, read how to choose a private habit tracker with no account.

## FAQ

What is a good alternative to HabitKit?
Habit Forever is the closest alternative, with a similar colorful grid, no account and on-device storage, plus limits for habits you want less of, weekly goals and Siri check-ins with an amount.

Is HabitKit free?
HabitKit is free to use, with a Pro upgrade available as a monthly, yearly or lifetime purchase.

Can I import my HabitKit data into Habit Forever?
No, Habit Forever cannot import HabitKit data and only imports its own JSON backups.

Do HabitKit and Habit Forever need an account?
No, both apps work without an account and keep your habit data on your device.

Does Habit Forever have a lifetime option like HabitKit?
Yes, Habit Forever Pro is available as a one-time lifetime purchase as well as yearly and monthly plans.

# Habit tracker comparisons
URL: https://habitforever.app/compare/
Updated: 2026-11-18

Fair comparisons of habit tracker apps for iPhone. I make Habit Forever, so I say so up front, and I point out when another app is the better fit.

# Is there a Loop Habit Tracker for iPhone?
URL: https://habitforever.app/compare/loop-habit-tracker-iphone.html
Updated: 2026-11-18

No. Loop Habit Tracker is a free, open-source app for Android only, available on Google Play and F-Droid, and it has no official iOS version. On iPhone, HabitKit, Streaks and Habit Forever offer a similar no-account, visual approach.

There is no official Loop Habit Tracker for iPhone. Loop is a free, open-source Android app, distributed through Google Play and F-Droid, and its developer has not released an iOS version.

If you used Loop on Android and have moved to iPhone, or a friend recommended it, here is what Loop does well and which iPhone apps come closest.

## What Loop Habit Tracker is

Loop Habit Tracker is a well-loved habit tracker for Android. It is free and its source code is public on GitHub. You can install it from F-Droid or Google Play.

People like it because it is simple, private and honest about progress. Its history views show your check-ins as a calendar grid, so you can see months of effort at once.

## A note on apps with the same name

If you search the App Store for "Loop habit", you may see an app that uses a similar name. As far as we can tell, it is not made by Loop's developer and is not the open-source Android app. Check the developer name on any listing before you assume it is the same project.

## What to look for in an iPhone replacement

Most Loop users care about the same few things:

- No account. Loop never asked you to sign up.

- A history grid. A calendar or heatmap view of your check-ins.

- Flexible schedules, such as three times a week.

- Number habits, not just yes or no.

- A fair price, ideally with a one-time option.

No iPhone app is open source and free in exactly the way Loop is, so expect to make some trade-off.

## iPhone alternatives to Loop

 | | App | Account needed | Grid or heatmap | Pricing model

 | HabitKit | No (on device) | Yes, tile grid layouts | Free + Pro (monthly, yearly or lifetime)

 | Streaks | No (iCloud sync) | — | Paid upfront, no in-app purchases

 | Habit Forever | No (on device) | Yes, a contribution grid per habit | Free for 3 habits + Pro (yearly, monthly or lifetime)

### HabitKit

HabitKit is probably the closest in spirit: no account, data on the device, and grid layouts where each habit fills in tiles over time. It supports yes/no, count and amount habits, and is free with a Pro upgrade. Read our HabitKit alternative page for how it compares with Habit Forever.

### Streaks

Streaks is a polished, Apple Design Award-winning app you buy once, with no account and iCloud sync. It has an Apple Watch app and can complete habits automatically from Apple Health. If you want sync between your iPhone and iPad, it is a strong pick. See Streaks app alternative.

 

### Habit Forever

We make Habit Forever, so take this with that in mind. It shares several things Loop users tend to like:

- No account, and habit records and notes stay on your device.

- A colorful day-by-day grid for each habit, in the style of a GitHub contribution graph, plus current and best streak and consistency.

- Flexible goals: daily or weekly, on every day, weekdays or chosen days.

- Number habits with a number to reach, or a limit to stay under for things you want less of.

- Widgets and Siri: check in from the Home Screen or Lock Screen, or with the "Check In Habit" action.

It differs from Loop in important ways. It is not open source. It is free for up to three habits, and Habit Forever Pro (yearly, monthly or a one-time lifetime purchase) unlocks unlimited habits, deeper insights, widgets for every habit and JSON backup export and import. It has no Android version, so it will not help if you still use an Android phone too.

## Can you move your Loop data to iPhone?

To our knowledge, none of the apps above advertise an import from Loop. Habit Forever cannot import Loop data. Its import only reads its own JSON backups.

The practical route is to start fresh. If you want to keep your old record, save whatever export Loop offers on your Android phone, or take screenshots of your history. If a recent run matters to you, you can fill in past days in Habit Forever by tapping them in the habit's grid, but only do this for days you actually did.

A fresh start is not a loss. Habit research suggests that progress lives in the repetitions you have already made, not in a number on a screen; see what a broken streak really means.

## FAQ

Is Loop Habit Tracker available on iPhone?
No, Loop Habit Tracker is an Android-only app available on Google Play and F-Droid, and it has no official iOS version.

What is the closest iPhone app to Loop Habit Tracker?
HabitKit and Habit Forever are close in approach, because both work without an account, keep data on the device and show habits as a visual grid.

Is there a free open-source habit tracker for iPhone like Loop?
We are not aware of an open-source iPhone tracker as established as Loop, but several apps, including HabitKit and Habit Forever, have free tiers.

Can I import my Loop Habit Tracker data into Habit Forever?
No, Habit Forever does not support importing Loop data and can only import its own JSON backups.

Is the app called Loop on the App Store the same as Loop Habit Tracker?
Loop Habit Tracker's developer has not released an official iOS app, so check the developer name on any App Store listing that uses a similar name.

# Looking for a Streaks app alternative?
URL: https://habitforever.app/compare/streaks-app-alternative.html
Updated: 2026-11-18

Stay with Streaks if you rely on Apple Watch, Apple Health auto-complete or iCloud sync; it does those very well. Look at an alternative such as Habit Forever if you want number goals with limits, weekly targets, contribution grids, or a free tier to start.

Disclosure: we make Habit Forever, one of the alternatives on this page. We have tried to be fair to Streaks, which is a genuinely excellent app, and to say clearly when it is the better choice.

Streaks is one of the best-known habit trackers on iPhone. The best alternative depends on why you are looking: if it is Apple Watch or Health, there may be no reason to switch at all; if it is the kind of goals you can set, there might be.

## What Streaks does well

Streaks, by Crunchy Bagel, has earned its reputation:

- Pay once. It is a paid upfront app with no in-app purchases and no subscription.

- Apple Design Award. Its design has been recognised by Apple.

- Apple Health auto-complete. Habits such as steps or workouts can tick themselves off from your Health data.

- Apple Watch app. You can check off habits from your wrist.

- No account, with iCloud sync. Your habits sync across your Apple devices without signing up for anything.

- A focused list. Its App Store listing describes tracking up to 24 tasks, which keeps the app focused.

## When Streaks is the better choice

Honestly, stay with Streaks, or choose it, if:

- You wear an Apple Watch and want to log habits from it.

- You want habits to complete automatically from Apple Health, such as a step count or a workout.

- You use an iPhone and an iPad and want them synced through iCloud.

- You strongly prefer a single upfront purchase with nothing more to buy.

Habit Forever has no Apple Watch app, no Apple Health integration and no iCloud sync, so it cannot replace Streaks for any of these.

## Why people look for an alternative

The reasons we hear most often are about how habits are measured, not about quality:

- Wanting limits, not just targets: "under 2 hours of screen time" or "spend no more than a set amount".

- Wanting weekly targets that do not feel like a broken streak on rest days.

- Wanting to see a long history at a glance as a colored grid.

- Wanting to try properly for free before paying.

 

## Where Habit Forever fits

Habit Forever is a habit tracker for iPhone and iPad (iOS 17 or later). Here is what it offers that matters for the reasons above.

### Number goals: reach a number or stay under a limit

Track check-off habits or number habits in pages, glasses, minutes, distance, spending or your own unit. For each number habit, set a minimum ("at least 20 pages"), or a maximum for habits you want less of ("at most 2 hours").

### Daily or weekly targets

Choose every day, weekdays or specific days, or set a target for the week. A weekly habit's streak counts weeks, so a planned rest day is not a miss.

### Contribution grids, streaks and consistency

Each habit has a colorful day-by-day grid in the style of a GitHub contribution graph, with your current and best streak and a consistency figure. You can see progress across all your habits too, and fill in a past day you actually did.

### Widgets and Siri

Check in from Home Screen and Lock Screen widgets. Siri and Shortcuts support "Check In Habit" (with an optional amount and note), "Get Habit Streak" and "Open Habit".

### Free tier, then a lifetime option

It is free for up to three habits, with goals, reminders and notes. Habit Forever Pro adds unlimited habits, deeper insights, widgets for every habit and JSON backup export and import, as a yearly or monthly plan or a one-time lifetime purchase. Prices are shown in the app before you buy.

### Private by default

No account, and habit records and notes stay on your device.

## Other Streaks alternatives

If neither fits, HabitKit is a visual, no-account tracker with a lifetime option, and Habitify works across iOS, Android, Mac and the web with an account (see our Habitify alternative page). Our full comparison of the best habit tracker apps for iPhone covers nine apps. If what you want is mainly a better widget, see how to add a habit tracker widget on iPhone.

## FAQ

What is a good alternative to the Streaks app?
HabitKit and Habit Forever are good alternatives if you want a visual grid without an account, and Habitify suits you if you need Android, Mac or web access.

Is there a free alternative to Streaks?
Yes, Habit Forever is free for up to three habits, and HabitKit and Habitify also have free tiers.

Does Habit Forever work with Apple Watch like Streaks?
No, Habit Forever does not have an Apple Watch app, so Streaks is the better choice if you want to log habits from your wrist.

Can Habit Forever complete habits from Apple Health?
No, Habit Forever does not integrate with Apple Health, while Streaks can complete habits automatically from Health data.

Does Habit Forever have a one-time purchase like Streaks?
Habit Forever Pro is available as a one-time lifetime purchase as well as yearly or monthly plans, after a free tier of up to three habits.

# How to build a reading habit
URL: https://habitforever.app/guides/build-a-reading-habit.html
Updated: 2026-11-18

To build a reading habit, set a small daily minimum in pages or minutes, attach it to a fixed moment such as after dinner, and track it. Twelve books a year of about 300 pages works out to roughly 10 pages a day, which at an average reading speed is about 10 to 13 minutes.

"Read more" is one of the most common resolutions, and one of the easiest to drop, because it is not a habit yet; it is a wish. What turns it into a habit is a number small enough to hit on a tired day and a moment in the day it belongs to. I built number habits into Habit Forever for goals like this one, and this guide shows the math, the built-in options on iPhone, and how to set it up.

## From books per year to pages per day

Start from the goal you want and work backwards. Book lengths vary a lot, so the table assumes an average of 300 pages per book; swap in your own number if you read shorter or longer books.

 | | Books per year | Pages per year (300-page books) | Pages per day

 | 6 | 1,800 | about 5

 | 12 (one a month) | 3,600 | about 10

 | 24 (two a month) | 7,200 | about 20

 | 52 (one a week) | 15,600 | about 43

The formula is simple: books per year × pages per book ÷ 365. A book a month is just 10 pages a day. That is the surprising part for most people: the gap between "I never read" and "I read a book a month" is a quarter of an hour. The free reading goal calculator does the math for any goal, book length and reading speed.

### How long does a page take?

A 2019 meta-analysis by Marc Brysbaert, covering 190 studies and 18,573 participants, put the average silent reading rate of adults in English at about 238 words per minute for non-fiction and 260 for fiction. Most adults read English non-fiction at somewhere between 175 and 300 words per minute, and the paper notes that these estimates are lower than the figures often cited in scientific and popular writing.

How many words fit on a page depends on the book. If a page holds roughly 250 to 300 words, a page takes about one minute to a minute and a quarter at those speeds. So:

- 10 pages a day is roughly 10 to 13 minutes.

- 20 pages a day is roughly 20 to 25 minutes.

These are averages. Dense non-fiction, a second language or a book you are studying will be slower, and that is fine.

## Pages or minutes?

- Pages are easy to count and give a clear sense of progress through a book. They are unfair to dense books: 10 pages of philosophy is not 10 pages of a thriller.

- Minutes treat every book the same and suit audiobooks. They are harder to keep honest if you read with your phone nearby.

Pick one and stay with it for a month. If you switch between hard and easy books a lot, minutes are usually the better choice.

## Built-in options on iPhone

Apple Books has Reading Goals: it tracks how much you read in a day, your streak and how many books you have read this year, and it counts reading you do in the Books app. If you read e-books or audiobooks there, it is a good free tracker.

If you read paper books, a Kindle or another app, Books does not see that reading. A repeating reminder in Reminders ("Read 10 pages") or a paper log works; our printable habit tracker has a monthly grid you can fill in with page counts.

 

## Track reading as a number habit in Habit Forever

Habit Forever tracks reading wherever it happens, because you log the number yourself. Here is how to set it up:

- Add a new habit called "Read".

- Under Goal, choose Reach a number, set at least 10 (or your number), and pick the unit pages or minutes.

- Choose Each day, or Each week if your reading happens in bigger sessions; 70 pages a week gives you room for a busy Tuesday.

- Turn on One tap adds with 10, so a normal session is one tap and longer ones use the keypad.

- Set a reminder for your reading moment, such as 9 pm. It stays quiet on days you have already logged.

Several sessions in one day add up, so 5 pages on the train and 15 in bed count as 20. Each habit has a current and best streak, and a day-by-day grid that fills in the days you reached your number. You can add a note to a check-in, a good place for the book title or a line worth keeping. If you forgot to log yesterday, you can fill in any of the last 7 days.

To log without opening the app, make a shortcut with the Check In Habit action and set Amount to Ask Each Time; see how to log habits with Siri and Shortcuts.

## Tips that actually help

- Set a minimum, not a target. Ten pages is the floor. On good days you will read 40, and that is a bonus, not the new rule.

- Attach it to an anchor. "After I get into bed, I will read 10 pages" is a plan; "read more" is not. This is habit stacking.

- Keep the book where the anchor is. On your pillow, in your bag, next to the kettle.

- Give yourself permission to quit a book. A book you dread stalls the whole habit. Start another.

- Be patient. Research suggests habits take weeks to months to feel automatic; see how long it takes to form a habit.

## FAQ

How many pages a day to read 12 books a year?
About 10 pages a day, assuming books of around 300 pages: 12 × 300 = 3,600 pages, divided by 365 days.

How long does it take to read 10 pages?
Roughly 10 to 13 minutes at an average reading speed, based on average silent reading rates of about 238 to 260 words per minute and pages of about 250 to 300 words.

Should I track reading in pages or minutes?
Pages are easy to count and show progress through a book, while minutes treat dense and light books the same and suit audiobooks.

Can Apple Books track my reading habit?
Yes, Apple Books Reading Goals tracks daily reading, streaks and books read this year, but only for reading done in the Books app.

## Sources

- Brysbaert, M. (2019). How many words do we read per minute? A review and meta-analysis of reading rate. Journal of Memory and Language, 109, 104047.

- Apple Books: Reading Goals

- Apple Support: Create reminders on iPhone

# Habit stacking: how it works and how to track it
URL: https://habitforever.app/guides/habit-stacking.html
Updated: 2026-11-18

Habit stacking means attaching a new habit to something you already do every day, using a sentence like "After I pour my morning coffee, I will write one line in my journal." The existing routine becomes the reminder, so you rely less on memory and motivation.

Habit stacking is one of the most practical ideas in the habit world, and also one of the most loosely credited. Below I explain where it comes from, with the sources, how to write a good stack, and how I would track one on iPhone.

## Where the idea comes from

Three names come up, and each deserves credit for a different part.

- BJ Fogg, who directs the Behavior Design Lab at Stanford University, created the Tiny Habits method. In it you attach a new, very small behavior to a habit you already do, which he calls an anchor. The sequence is anchor, then tiny behavior, then a small celebration, written as a recipe: "After I…, I will…". His book is Tiny Habits: The Small Changes That Change Everything.

- S.J. Scott published a book called Habit Stacking in 2014 (subtitled 97 Small Life Changes That Take Five Minutes or Less, later revised), which helped popularize the term.

- James Clear brought it to a wide audience in Atomic Habits and on his website, with the formula "After [current habit], I will [new habit]." He credits the method to BJ Fogg's Tiny Habits program, notes that Fogg calls it anchoring, and credits S.J. Scott for the phrase "habit stacking".

Underneath all three is older research. Research by the psychologist Peter Gollwitzer showed that plans of the form "if situation Y, then I will do Z", which he called implementation intentions, help people follow through on what they intend; his 1999 paper in American Psychologist summarizes it. Clear describes habit stacking as a special form of implementation intention, where the situation is a habit you already have.

## How to build a habit stack

### 1. Pick a precise anchor

The anchor should be something you do every day without thinking, and it should happen at a clear moment. Tiny Habits material from Fogg makes the point well: "After I finish dinner" is a weak anchor because there is no precise moment when dinner ends, while "After I take my plate into the kitchen" works. Good anchors include:

- After I put my feet on the floor in the morning

- After I pour my first coffee

- After I sit down at my desk

- After I plug in my phone at night

### 2. Make the new habit tiny

Start with a version you could do on your worst day: one push-up, one line in a journal, open the book. You can always do more, but the stack should never depend on having energy. "After I pour my coffee, I will write one line" survives a bad morning; "I will journal for 20 minutes" often does not.

### 3. Write the sentence down

Use the exact formula: "After I [anchor], I will [new habit]." Saying where and when out loud is what turns a wish into a plan.

### 4. Mark it straight away

Fogg's method puts a small celebration right after the behavior, because a good feeling helps the habit stick. A quiet "yes", a smile, or ticking it off counts. That last one is where a tracker earns its place.

### 5. Add the next link later

Once a stack feels automatic, the new habit can become the anchor for another: coffee, then one journal line, then two minutes of stretching. Add links one at a time, and only when the previous one is steady.

## Use your iPhone as the anchor

Some of the best anchors are things your iPhone already notices, and the Shortcuts app can turn them into a prompt with a personal automation. Triggers include your alarm being stopped, your wake-up time, arriving home, CarPlay disconnecting and your phone being connected to a charger. An automation could show a notification such as "Stretch for two minutes" when you stop your morning alarm.

Reminders works too: a repeating reminder at the time your anchor usually happens.

 

## How I would track a stack in Habit Forever

Habit Forever has no special "stack" feature; it does not need one. A stack is a few habits done in order, and the app handles each one well:

- Name the habit with its anchor. "Journal after coffee" puts the whole recipe on your Today screen.

- Put the stack in order. Reorder your habits (in Settings) so they appear in the order you do them.

- Time the reminder to the anchor. Set the habit's reminder for when the anchor usually happens. Reminders only arrive on the habit's days and stay quiet once you have checked in.

- Tick it off as the celebration. A tap on the habit, a widget on the Lock Screen, or "Check in on Habit Forever" to Siri. See how to log habits with Siri and Shortcuts.

- Use a number when the habit grows. Start with a check-off, then switch to a number goal such as at least 2 minutes or 5 pages when the tiny version is easy.

The free version tracks up to three habits, which is a good size for a first stack. Each habit keeps its own streak and day-by-day grid, so you can see which link in the chain is solid and which keeps slipping. To picture a year of a stack, try the habit grid maker.

## Common mistakes

- A vague anchor. "In the morning" is not an anchor. "After I switch off the kettle" is.

- An anchor that does not happen every day. If you only go to the office three days a week, "after I sit at my desk" will miss the other days. Use a schedule for those days, or pick a daily anchor. See weekly habit goals.

- Stacking too much at once. Five new habits after coffee is a routine you have to remember, not a stack.

- Quitting after a miss. One missed day does little harm; read what to do when you miss a day.

How long until a stack feels automatic varies a lot from person to person; how long it takes to form a habit covers the research.

## FAQ

What is habit stacking?
Habit stacking means attaching a new habit to something you already do every day, using a sentence like "After I pour my morning coffee, I will write one line in my journal."

Who came up with habit stacking?
BJ Fogg created the method of anchoring a tiny new behavior to an existing habit in Tiny Habits, S.J. Scott helped popularize the term with his 2014 book Habit Stacking, and James Clear brought it to a wide audience in Atomic Habits.

What is the habit stacking formula?
James Clear's formula is "After [current habit], I will [new habit]," which follows BJ Fogg's Tiny Habits recipe "After I…, I will…".

Is habit stacking backed by research?
It builds on research into implementation intentions, if-then plans studied by Peter Gollwitzer, which help people follow through on what they intend.

## Sources

- Tiny Habits (BJ Fogg): creator of the method, Behavior Design Lab at Stanford

- Tiny Habits: Getting Started (Tiny Habits material by BJ Fogg and Linda Fogg Phillips, adapted by Stanford Medicine's ASCEND project)

- James Clear: Habit Stacking: How to Build New Habits by Taking Advantage of Old Ones

- S.J. Scott, Habit Stacking (2014), Open Library record

- Gollwitzer, P. M. (1999). Implementation intentions: Strong effects of simple plans. American Psychologist, 54(7), 493–503.

- Apple Support: Event triggers in Shortcuts

# How to add a habit tracker widget to your iPhone
URL: https://habitforever.app/guides/habit-tracker-widget-iphone.html
Updated: 2026-10-22

Touch and hold your Home Screen until the apps jiggle, tap Edit, then Add Widget, and pick your habit tracker. For the Lock Screen, touch and hold it, tap Customize, choose the Lock Screen, then tap Add Widgets.

A habit tracker widget puts today's habits where you already look dozens of times a day. To add one, touch and hold an empty part of your Home Screen, tap Edit at the top, tap Add Widget, and choose your habit app. Lock Screen widgets are added from the Customize screen instead.

The exact wording has shifted a little between iOS versions, so the steps below cover iOS 17, iOS 18 and iOS 26.

## Add a widget to the Home Screen

### iOS 18 and iOS 26

- Go to the Home Screen page where you want the widget.

- Touch and hold the background until the apps begin to jiggle.

- Tap Edit at the top of the screen, then tap Add Widget.

- Scroll or search for your habit tracker, tap it, then swipe through the sizes and styles.

- When you see the size you want, tap Add Widget.

- While the apps are still jiggling, drag the widget into place, then tap Done.

### iOS 17

The steps are the same, except that after the apps jiggle you tap the add button (the plus sign) at the top of the screen to open the widget gallery.

On newer iOS versions the Edit control may appear as a button icon rather than the word "Edit". It sits in the same place at the top of the screen.

Tip: to change which habit a widget shows, touch and hold the widget, tap Edit Widget, and choose a habit. You can also stack widgets on top of each other to save space.

## Add a widget to the Lock Screen

Lock Screen widgets have been available since iOS 16 and are small and monochrome: a circle, a rectangle, or a single line of text above the clock.

- Wake your iPhone and unlock it with Face ID or Touch ID, but stay on the Lock Screen.

- Touch and hold the Lock Screen until the Customize button appears, then tap it.

- If you are asked to choose, pick the Lock Screen.

- Tap Add Widgets, or tap the widget area below the time.

- Tap or drag the habit widget you want. If there is no room, remove another widget first.

- Close the widget list, then tap Done.

The single-line widget lives in the spot next to the date above the clock; tap the date while customizing to change it.

## What makes a good habit widget

Not all habit widgets are equal. Before you choose an app for its widget, check three things:

- Can you check in from the widget? Since iOS 17, widgets can run small actions without opening the app. A widget that only displays your streak still makes you open the app to log.

- Does it work on the Lock Screen? A Lock Screen widget is visible every time you pick up your phone, even before you unlock it.

- Is it free? Some apps limit widgets to paid plans. Check before you build your routine around one.

 

## Habit Forever's widgets

We make Habit Forever, a habit tracker for iPhone and iPad, so here is exactly what its widgets do.

### The Habit widget (one habit)

- Home Screen sizes: small and medium. It shows one habit's streak, its week and recent activity.

- Lock Screen sizes: circular, rectangular and inline. The rectangular version shows the habit, your streak, dots for the week, and a check-in button.

- One-tap check-in: tap the circle on the widget to log today without opening the app. For a number habit, a tap logs the fixed amount you chose for a single tap, such as one glass.

Habits you want less of, set with a "Stay under" goal, are logged in the app instead, so a stray tap can never record a slip.

### The All Habits widget

Medium and large sizes show your whole day at a glance so you can check in on your habits without opening the app; the large size also shows how many of today's habits are done. It is part of Habit Forever Pro.

### Free and Pro

- Free: the Habit widget works for your first habit, on both the Home Screen and the Lock Screen.

- Habit Forever Pro: widgets for every habit, plus the All Habits widget. Pro is available yearly, monthly or as a one-time lifetime purchase; prices are shown in the app before you buy.

The free plan also covers up to three habits with goals, reminders and notes, so you can try the widget properly before deciding anything.

## If your habit widget is not updating

- Open the app once after installing or updating it. Widgets read data the app has saved.

- Check that the habit is due today. A habit scheduled for other days will not offer a check-in.

- Remove and re-add the widget if it shows an old habit after you renamed or archived it.

- Turn off Low Power Mode briefly. iOS may refresh widgets less often to save battery.

A widget works best alongside a habit you can actually keep. If you are just getting started, read how to track habits on iPhone, or see how a number habit and a widget combine in our guide to tracking water intake on iPhone. For hands-free check-ins, see how to log habits with Siri and Shortcuts.

## FAQ

Can I check off a habit from the iPhone Lock Screen?
Yes, on iOS 17 or later a Lock Screen widget with a button can log a habit without opening the app, and Habit Forever's rectangular Lock Screen widget includes a check-in button.

Why can't I find my habit app in the widget gallery?
Open the app at least once after installing it, then search for it by name in the widget gallery, because widgets only appear after the app has run.

How do I change which habit a widget shows?
Touch and hold the widget, tap Edit Widget, and choose a different habit from the list.

Are Habit Forever's widgets free?
The Habit widget is free for your first habit on both the Home Screen and Lock Screen, while widgets for every habit and the All Habits widget come with Habit Forever Pro.

Can a widget log a number, like glasses of water?
Yes, in Habit Forever a tap on the widget logs the fixed amount you chose for a single tap in that habit, such as one glass.

## Sources

- Apple Support: How to add and edit widgets on your iPhone

- Apple Support: Add, edit, and remove widgets on iPhone

- Apple Support: Create a custom Lock Screen on iPhone

# A habit tracker without a subscription
URL: https://habitforever.app/guides/habit-tracker-without-subscription.html
Updated: 2026-11-18

You can track habits on iPhone without a subscription in three ways: free built-in tools (Reminders, Notes, paper), an app you pay for once, or an app's free tier. Habit Forever is free for up to three habits with no time limit, and its Pro upgrade has a one-time lifetime option next to yearly and monthly plans.

I make Habit Forever, and I get asked about subscriptions more than anything else. That is fair: a habit tracker is something you hope to use for years, and a monthly charge for a checklist can feel wrong. So here are the honest options, starting with the ones that cost nothing.

## Free options already on your iPhone

- Reminders. A repeating reminder that you tick off each day is the closest thing iPhone has to a built-in habit tracker. It costs nothing and syncs through iCloud if you use it. It has no streaks, no counts and no history you can read at a glance. My guide on how to track habits on iPhone walks through the steps.

- Notes. A checklist or a small table with dates down the side. Flexible and private, but nothing reminds you and nothing adds up.

- Paper. A grid on the fridge is hard to ignore. Our printable habit tracker gives you a ready-made monthly sheet for free.

If you only want to take a vitamin every morning, any of these is enough. You do not need to pay anyone.

## How habit tracker apps charge

Apps that do more (streaks, number goals, widgets, reminders per habit) tend to use one of four models. Here is how the apps in our comparison of iPhone habit trackers describe their pricing on their own pages:

 | | Model | What it means | Examples

 | Paid upfront | Pay once to download, nothing more | Streaks (no in-app purchases)

 | Free tier + lifetime option | Use the free part for as long as you like, and buy the upgrade once or as a subscription | HabitKit, Habitify, Habit Forever

 | Subscription or lifetime, no free tier stated | A subscription, with a one-time purchase also offered | Everyday

 | Subscription | Recurring payment, with limited free use | (Not Boring) Habits

Way of Life and Strides are free with in-app purchases. Pricing changes, so check the App Store listing before you buy. I never print prices on this site for that reason; the app shows the current price before you pay.

## What Habit Forever gives you for free

The free version is not a trial. There is no countdown and no account to create. You get up to three habits with the core of the app:

- Check-off habits, or number habits such as pages, glasses, minutes or spending.

- Goals: reach a number, or stay under a limit, each day or each week, on every day or chosen days.

- Reminders per habit, which stay quiet on days you already checked in.

- Notes on check-ins, current and best streaks, and a colorful day-by-day grid for each habit.

Habit records and notes are stored on your device. There is no iCloud sync.

## The lifetime option

Habit Forever Pro adds unlimited habits, deeper insights (your strongest days, your usual time of day, month by month), widgets for every habit, and backup export and import. You can buy it yearly, monthly, or once as a lifetime purchase. Lifetime means you pay one time and Pro stays on your Apple Account, with no subscription and nothing to renew. If you get a new iPhone, you restore the purchase with the same Apple Account.

Purchases are handled by Apple, so a yearly or monthly plan is cancelled the usual way in your iPhone's Settings, under your name and then Subscriptions.

 

## Is three habits enough?

Some people tell me three free habits is too few, and for someone tracking ten things it is. But for most people starting out, three is a good number to begin with rather than a cage. In my experience, starting with a dozen habits on day one is a fast way to stop tracking any of them. Here is how I would pick the three:

- One habit that matters most. The change you would be proudest of in six months: reading, exercise, sleep.

- One easy win. Something small you will almost always do, like taking a vitamin or stepping outside after breakfast. Seeing a streak build keeps you opening the app.

- One thing to do less of. Screen time, coffee or daily spending, with a limit instead of a target. See how to track a habit you want to do less.

Make each one specific, such as "read 10 pages after dinner" rather than "read more". If a habit needs to happen a few times a week rather than daily, one habit with a weekly goal covers it; see weekly habit goals.

When a habit feels automatic, you can archive it. Its history is kept, and on the free version it no longer counts toward your three, so a new habit can take its place. Bringing an archived habit back onto the Today screen is a Pro feature, so archive the ones you are truly done tracking.

## Which option should you choose?

- One or two simple daily habits: Reminders or paper. Free, no app needed.

- Up to three habits with streaks and number goals: Habit Forever's free version, with no time limit.

- More than three habits, no subscription: an app with a one-time purchase, such as Habit Forever's lifetime option, or Streaks if you want an Apple Watch app.

- Several devices, including Android or the web: an app with account sync, such as Habitify. See my Habitify comparison.

## FAQ

Is there a habit tracker with no subscription?
Yes: Streaks is paid upfront with no in-app purchases, and HabitKit, Habitify, Everyday and Habit Forever offer a one-time lifetime option next to their subscriptions.

Is Habit Forever free?
Habit Forever is free for up to three habits with no time limit, including goals, reminders, notes, streaks and grids.

What does Habit Forever's lifetime option include?
Lifetime means you pay one time and Pro stays on your Apple Account, with unlimited habits, deeper insights, widgets for every habit and backup export and import.

Can I track habits on iPhone for free without an app?
Yes, a repeating reminder in the Reminders app, a Notes checklist or a printed paper tracker all work for free.

# How long does it take to form a habit?
URL: https://habitforever.app/guides/how-long-to-form-a-habit.html
Updated: 2026-11-18

Usually about two months, but with a very wide range. In the best-known study, the median time for a new daily habit to feel close to automatic was 66 days, with individuals ranging from 18 to 254 days.

It takes about two months for a typical new habit to become automatic, not 21 days. A 2010 study by Phillippa Lally and colleagues found a median of 66 days, and a 2024 review of 20 studies found medians of 59 to 66 days, with individual times ranging from a few days to most of a year.

That range matters more than the headline number. Here is what the research actually measured, where the 21-day figure came from, and how to use the findings.

## The 66-day study (Lally et al., 2010)

Researchers at University College London asked 96 volunteers to pick one new daily behavior tied to a cue, such as eating a piece of fruit with lunch or going for a run before dinner. Every day for 84 days, participants rated how automatic the behavior felt, using questions such as whether they did it without having to consciously remember.

For most people, automaticity rose quickly at first and then levelled off, like a curve approaching a ceiling. The researchers measured how long it took each person to reach 95% of their own plateau.

- The model fitted the data well for 39 participants, not all 96.

- Among them, the median was 66 days.

- The range was 18 to 254 days. Because the study ran for 84 days, the longer times were estimated by extending each person's curve, not observed directly.

- The behaviors people chose differed in effort, and how long they took to become automatic differed widely too.

One finding is especially useful: missing a single opportunity did not materially affect the habit-forming process. A missed day is not a reset. We cover that in detail in what to do when you miss a day.

## The 2024 review: 20 studies, 2,601 people

A systematic review by Singh and colleagues, published in Healthcare in 2024, pulled together 20 studies with 2,601 participants looking at how long health habits take to form.

- Median times ranged from 59 to 66 days across the studies that reported them.

- Mean times were longer, 106 to 154 days, because a few people who took a very long time pull the average up.

- Individual times ranged from 4 to 335 days.

The authors are cautious. Only a few studies reported timing at all, and most carried a high risk of bias. So treat "about two months" as a reasonable expectation, not a promise. That is also why we say median rather than average: the median is the middle person, while the average is stretched by the slow cases.

## Where the 21-day myth comes from

The 21-day figure is commonly traced to Psycho-Cybernetics, a 1960 book by plastic surgeon Maxwell Maltz. He observed that people seemed to need a minimum of about 21 days to adjust to a change, such as a new face after surgery or the loss of a limb.

Over the decades, "a minimum of about 21 days" to adjust appears to have been shortened into "it takes 21 days to form a habit". That was never a research finding. Three weeks can be a fine first milestone, but if a habit still feels like effort on day 22, nothing has gone wrong.

## What makes a habit form faster or slower

- Complexity. A glass of water after waking forms faster than a 30-minute workout.

- A stable cue. Linking the habit to the same time, place or existing routine ("after I pour my coffee") helps it become automatic. This is the idea behind habit stacking.

- Repetition in a similar context. Automaticity grows with repetitions, so a daily habit usually forms faster than a weekly one.

- Personal differences. The spread from 18 to 254 days shows how much people vary. Compare yourself with your own last month, not with a number.

## Estimate your own timeline

If you want a rough date to aim for, our habit formation calculator uses these research figures to give you a rough window for when a habit might start to feel automatic. Treat the result as a guide, not a deadline.

 

## How to get through the first two months

The hard part is the long middle, when the novelty has gone and the habit is not yet automatic. A few things help:

- Make it small. Two pages a day that you actually read beats twenty you skip; our guide to building a reading habit does the math.

- Track it visibly. Watching a day-by-day grid fill in gives you proof of progress before the habit feels easy. Habit Forever shows a colorful grid for each habit, along with your current and best streak and a consistency figure.

- Use weekly targets where daily is unrealistic. If you train three times a week, a weekly goal keeps rest days from breaking your record. Habit Forever supports daily and weekly goals.

- Keep a reminder at your cue time. A reminder tied to your routine prompts you until the cue does the work by itself.

- Plan for the miss. You will miss days. The research says one miss does not undo your progress, so just do the next one.

New to tracking? Start with how to track habits on iPhone.

## FAQ

Does it really take 21 days to form a habit?
No, research suggests a median of about 59 to 66 days, and the 21-day figure is commonly traced to a 1960 observation by Maxwell Maltz about adjusting to change, not to habit research.

What did the 66-day study find?
Lally and colleagues found that among 39 participants whose data fitted their model well, the median time to reach 95% of their automaticity plateau was 66 days, ranging from 18 to 254 days.

Why do some habits take almost a year?
Harder or less frequent behaviors, weaker cues and individual differences all slow automaticity down, and the 2024 review found individual times as long as 335 days.

Does missing a day reset habit formation?
No, in the Lally study missing a single opportunity did not materially affect the habit-forming process.

Is the median the same as the average time?
No, the median is the middle value, while the average is pulled up by people who take a very long time, which is why the 2024 review reports means of 106 to 154 days but medians of 59 to 66 days.

## Sources

- Lally P, van Jaarsveld CHM, Potts HWW, Wardle J. How are habits formed: Modelling habit formation in the real world. European Journal of Social Psychology, 2010.

- Singh B, et al. Systematic review of the time taken to form health behaviour habits. Healthcare 12(23):2488, 2024.

# How to track habits on iPhone
URL: https://habitforever.app/guides/how-to-track-habits-on-iphone.html
Updated: 2026-11-18

You can track habits on iPhone with the built-in Reminders app (a repeating reminder you tick off), Calendar, or a Notes checklist. When you want streaks, number goals and a history you can actually read, a dedicated habit tracker app does the job better.

The simplest way to track a habit on iPhone is a repeating reminder in the Reminders app: you tick it off each day and it comes back tomorrow. That works for one or two habits. Once you want to see a streak, count glasses or pages, or look back over a month, a dedicated habit tracker is the better tool.

Below are four ways to do it, starting with what is already on your phone, with the honest limits of each.

## 1. The Reminders app (repeating reminders)

Reminders comes with every iPhone and is the closest thing to a built-in habit tracker.

- Open Reminders and create a list, for example "Habits".

- Add a reminder such as "Read 10 pages".

- Open the reminder's details, give it a date and time, and choose a repeat option such as daily, or custom days.

- Tick it off when you have done it. The next one appears for the following day.

What it does well: it is free, it syncs through iCloud if you use it, and the notification arrives at the time you choose. Reminders also has widgets, so you can tick items off from the Home Screen.

Where it falls short: a repeating reminder has no memory you can see. There is no streak, no calendar of the days you did it, and no way to say "I drank 6 of 8 glasses". If you miss a day, the old reminder simply stays overdue. Apple notes that future instances of a repeating reminder can only be completed after the current one is marked complete, which makes catching up awkward.

## 2. The Calendar app

Some people create a repeating all-day event called "Workout" and rename or recolor it on the days they actually did it. Others keep a separate calendar just for habits and add an event after each one.

What it does well: the month view gives you a visual record, and it costs nothing.

Where it falls short: Calendar is built for appointments, so logging takes several taps, it cannot count anything, and your habit entries clutter your real schedule unless you hide that calendar.

## 3. A Notes checklist or a paper tracker

In the Notes app you can make a checklist with one line per day, or a table with your habits across the top and dates down the side. Paper works the same way: a grid on the fridge, filled in with a pen.

What it does well: it is completely flexible, private, and satisfying to fill in. Paper in particular is hard to ignore when it is on the wall. If you like this route, our printable habit tracker gives you a ready-made monthly grid.

Where it falls short: nothing reminds you, nothing adds up your streak, and a note does not tell you that you did best on Tuesdays. You also have to start a fresh sheet every month.

## What the built-in options miss

Built-in apps are fine for a quick start. In practice, people who stick with tracking usually want a few things that none of them offer together:

- A visible streak and a best streak, so a run of good days feels worth protecting.

- Number goals, such as 8 glasses of water, 20 pages or 30 minutes, not just done or not done.

- Limits for habits you want less of, such as under 2 hours of screen time (see how to track a habit you want to do less).

- Weekly targets, such as the gym three times a week, without breaking a daily streak on rest days (see weekly habit goals).

- A history at a glance, so you can see a whole year of effort in one picture.

- Quick logging from a widget or Siri, because every extra tap is a reason to skip.

 

## 4. A dedicated habit tracker app

A habit tracker is built around exactly the list above. We make one, Habit Forever, so here is what it does and does not do, plainly.

- Check-off or number habits. Tick a habit off, or count pages, glasses, minutes, distance, spending or your own unit.

- Goals that fit the habit. Reach a number (at least 20 pages), stay under a limit for habits you want less of (at most 2 hours), or just check it off. Goals can be per day or per week, on every day, weekdays or chosen days.

- Streaks and grids. Each habit shows its current and best streak, a consistency figure and a colorful day-by-day grid in the style of a GitHub contribution graph.

- Reminders per habit, notes on check-ins, and the option to fill in a past day you actually did.

- Widgets and Siri. Check in from Home Screen and Lock Screen widgets, or use the "Check In Habit" action in Siri and Shortcuts. See how to log habits with Siri and Shortcuts.

- No account. Your habit records and notes stay on your device.

It runs on iPhone and iPad with iOS 17 or later. It is free for up to three habits; Habit Forever Pro adds unlimited habits, deeper insights, widgets for every habit and backup export and import. It does not have an Apple Watch app, iCloud sync or Apple Health integration, so if any of those matter to you, compare a few options first in our guide to the best habit tracker apps for iPhone. If you would rather not subscribe, read about habit trackers without a subscription.

## How to start tracking without giving up

- Start with one to three habits. More than that in week one is the most common reason people stop.

- Make each habit specific. "Read 10 pages after dinner" beats "read more" (see how to build a reading habit). Tying a habit to something you already do is called habit stacking. The reading goal calculator turns a yearly book goal into pages a day, and the habit cost calculator shows what a habit you want less of costs you in a year.

- Put the tracker where you will see it. A Home Screen or Lock Screen widget turns a glance at your phone into a reminder. See how to add a habit tracker widget.

- Expect it to take a while. Research suggests habits take weeks to months to feel automatic, not 21 days. Our guide on how long it takes to form a habit explains the numbers.

- Do not quit after a miss. One missed day does little harm; read what to do when you miss a day.

## Which method should you choose?

 | | Method | Best for | Main limit

 | Reminders app | One or two simple daily habits | No streaks, no history, no counts

 | Calendar app | A rough monthly picture | Slow to log, clutters your schedule

 | Notes or paper | Total flexibility, offline | No reminders or automatic streaks

 | Habit tracker app | Several habits, number goals, long-term progress | One more app to choose and learn

If you only want a nudge to take a vitamin, Reminders is enough. If you want to see your progress build over months, a tracker is worth it.

## FAQ

Does iPhone have a built-in habit tracker?
No, iPhone has no dedicated habit tracker, but a repeating reminder in the Reminders app works as a simple one because you tick it off and it returns the next day.

Can I track habits in Apple Health?
Apple Health records health data such as steps, sleep and water, but it does not track general habits like reading or journaling with streaks.

Is a habit tracker app better than paper?
Paper is flexible and hard to ignore on a wall, while an app adds reminders, automatic streaks, number goals and a long history, so the better choice depends on which of those you need.

Do I need an account to track habits on iPhone?
Not always; Reminders, Notes and some habit trackers, including Habit Forever, work without creating an account.

How many habits should I track at once?
Starting with one to three habits makes it much easier to keep going, and you can add more once those feel routine.

## Sources

- Apple Support: Use reminders on iPhone

- Apple Support: Create reminders on iPhone
