# How to log habits with Siri and Shortcuts
URL: https://habitforever.app/guides/log-habits-with-siri-shortcuts.html
Updated: 2026-11-18

To log a habit with Siri, use a habit tracker that offers App Shortcuts: with Habit Forever, say "Check in on Habit Forever" and Siri asks which habit. In the Shortcuts app you can go further and log a habit, with an amount and a note, from the Action button, an NFC tag or an automation that runs at a set time or place.

Every tap between you and a check-in is a reason to skip it. I built Siri and Shortcuts support into Habit Forever for exactly that reason, and this guide shows what iPhone itself offers first, then the exact phrases and actions the app adds.

## What iPhone gives you for free

iPhone has no habit log of its own, but it has three tools that any app can plug into:

- Siri can run any shortcut in your collection when you say its name.

- The Shortcuts app shows built-in shortcuts from your apps in its App Shortcuts area, and lets you combine their actions into your own shortcuts.

- Automations run a shortcut when something happens: a time of day, arriving at or leaving a place, scanning an NFC tag, opening an app, connecting to Wi-Fi or Bluetooth, a Focus turning on, your alarm being stopped and more.

You can also start any shortcut with a physical gesture: the Action button on iPhone 15 Pro and later (Settings > Action Button, swipe to Shortcut, then Choose a Shortcut), or Back Tap, which runs a shortcut when you double-tap or triple-tap the back of your iPhone (Settings > Accessibility > Touch > Back Tap).

If all you want is a spoken nudge, Siri can already create a reminder for you, which works as a simple tracker; see how to track habits on iPhone. To actually log a habit and keep a streak, you need an app that provides the actions.

## Habit Forever's Siri phrases

These work as soon as the app is installed. There is nothing to set up. Ask Siri:

 | | Say | What happens

 | "Check in on Habit Forever""Log a habit in Habit Forever""Track my habit in Habit Forever" | Siri asks which habit, checks it in for today and tells you your streak

 | "Show my streak in Habit Forever""What's my streak in Habit Forever" | Siri asks which habit and reads its current streak

 | "Open a habit in Habit Forever" | Opens that habit in the app

After a check-in Siri answers with something like "Checked in on Read. You're on a 5-day streak!" For a habit with a weekly goal, the streak is counted in weeks. Your Home Screen and Lock Screen widgets update straight away.

## The three Shortcuts actions

In the Shortcuts app, Habit Forever adds three actions you can use in your own shortcuts and automations:

- Check In Habit: marks a habit as done for today, without opening the app. It has two optional fields: Amount, for number habits (3 glasses, 25 minutes, 20 pages), and Note, which is saved with the check-in in that habit's history.

- Get Habit Streak: returns the current streak for a habit as a number you can use in the next action, for example in a notification.

- Open Habit: opens a specific habit in the app.

For a number habit, fill in Amount so the check-in adds to your total. If you leave it empty, the check-in marks the day as done without a number. You can also set Amount to Ask Each Time, so the shortcut asks you how much when it runs.

## Log a specific habit in one sentence

The built-in phrases always ask which habit. To skip that question, make a shortcut for one habit and give it a short name:

- Open the Shortcuts app and create a new shortcut.

- Add the Check In Habit action from Habit Forever and choose the habit, for example "Drink water".

- Set Amount to 1 if it is a number habit.

- Name the shortcut "Log water".

Now "Hey Siri, log water" checks it in. The same shortcut can go on the Action button or Back Tap, so one press logs a glass. Not sure how many glasses to aim for? The water intake calculator gives you a starting point.

 

## Log habits automatically

Automations are where Shortcuts shines for habits. A few that work well with Check In Habit:

- NFC tag: stick a cheap NFC tag on your vitamin bottle or by the door and check in when you tap your iPhone on it. Apple notes that not all devices support NFC.

- Arrive: check in "Gym" when you arrive at the gym's address.

- App: check in "Read" when you open your e-book app, if opening it really means you read.

- Time of Day: at 9 pm, run Get Habit Streak and show a notification with the number, as an evening nudge.

Be honest with yourself about automatic check-ins. Arriving at the gym is not the same as working out, so for habits like that I prefer an automation that asks first, or the Action button.

### How to create an automation

The steps changed in iOS 27, so here are both versions from Apple's Shortcuts guide:

- iOS 26 and earlier: in Shortcuts, tap Automation (then the add button if you already have automations), tap Create Personal Automation, choose a trigger such as Time of Day or Arrive, set its options, tap Next, and add the Check In Habit action.

- iOS 27: open the shortcut you made (for example "Log water"), tap Edit, then Automation, and choose a trigger.

By default an automation asks before it runs. You can set it to run without asking; in iOS 27 that is under the shortcut's Info button, Privacy, Allow Running When Locked. Automations are specific to one device.

## What to know before you rely on it

- Check In Habit always logs for today. To fill in a day you missed, open the app; Habit Forever lets you add a check-in for any of the last 7 days.

- Siri needs to be turned on, and when your iPhone is locked, Siri may ask you to unlock it before a shortcut that opens an app.

- Habit Forever has no Apple Watch app, so these shortcuts run on iPhone and iPad.

Siri and widgets work well together: Siri for hands-free moments, a widget for a one-tap glance. See how to add a habit tracker widget, or how to track water intake on iPhone for a number habit that suits both.

## FAQ

Can I log a habit with Siri?
Yes, with an app that offers App Shortcuts: in Habit Forever, say "Check in on Habit Forever" and Siri asks which habit, checks it in and tells you your streak.

Can Siri log an amount, like glasses of water?
Yes, the Check In Habit action in Shortcuts has an optional Amount field, so a shortcut can log 1 glass, 20 pages or 25 minutes, or ask you each time.

Can I check in a habit automatically?
Yes, a Shortcuts automation can run Check In Habit at a time of day, when you arrive somewhere, open an app or scan an NFC tag.

Does it work from the Action button?
Yes, on iPhone 15 Pro and later you can set the Action button to run a shortcut that contains the Check In Habit action.

# Missed a day? What a broken habit streak really means
URL: https://habitforever.app/guides/missed-a-day-habit-streak.html
Updated: 2026-11-18

One missed day does not undo a habit. In the best-known study of habit formation, missing a single opportunity did not materially affect progress; what matters is getting back to it the next time.

If you missed a day and broke your habit streak, your habit is almost certainly fine. Research on habit formation found that a single missed opportunity did not materially affect how automatic a behavior became, so the best move is simply to do it again today.

The streak counter went back to zero. Your progress did not. Here is why, and how to think about streaks so one miss does not turn into a week off.

## What the research says about missing a day

In a 2010 study by Phillippa Lally and colleagues, volunteers repeated a chosen daily behavior and rated how automatic it felt every day for 84 days. Some people missed days along the way. The researchers found that missing one opportunity did not materially affect the habit-forming process.

That makes sense when you think about how a habit forms. Automaticity builds from many repetitions of a behavior in response to the same cue. One gap among dozens of repetitions is a small dent, not a demolition. A streak counter, by contrast, treats a single miss as total failure, which is why breaking one feels so much worse than it is.

For the full picture of how long habits take, see how long it takes to form a habit.

## The "never miss twice" rule

A popular rule of thumb, made widely known by James Clear in his book Atomic Habits, is "never miss twice". Missing once is an accident; missing twice is the start of a new pattern.

It is a rule of thumb, not a research finding, but it fits the evidence well. One miss barely matters. A string of misses means you are no longer repeating the behavior, and that is when a habit fades. So the day after a miss is the most important day to show up, even if you only do a tiny version: one page, one push-up, one glass of water.

## Consistency matters more than a perfect streak

A streak counts how many days in a row you have done something. Consistency asks a better question: out of the days you planned to do it, how many did you?

 | | | Streak | Consistency

 | What it measures | Days in a row | Share of planned days completed

 | After one miss | Drops to zero | Dips slightly

 | Good for | Motivation in the moment | An honest long-term picture

 | Risk | "I broke it, so why bother?" | Less exciting day to day

If you went to the gym 26 of 30 planned days, you did very well, even if your current streak is 3. Both numbers are useful. Just do not let the streak be the only one you look at.

## What to do after a missed day

- Do the habit today, even a smaller version. Restarting is the whole game.

- Look at why you missed. Travel, a late night, no time slot? Adjust the plan, not your opinion of yourself.

- Consider a weekly target. If "every day" does not match your life, "four times a week" may be more honest and much easier to keep.

- Schedule rest days on purpose. A habit set for chosen days does not count planned days off as misses.

- Record the truth. If you did the habit but forgot to log it, fill it in. If you did not, leave it blank. An honest record is more useful than a pretty one.

 

## How Habit Forever handles a missed day

We make Habit Forever, and we designed it so one miss does not wipe out the story of your effort.

- Current and best streak. Each habit shows both. When your current streak resets, your best streak stays, so you can see what you have already proved you can do.

- Consistency. Each habit shows how often you hit your planned days over recent weeks. Days you did not schedule the habit for are not counted against you.

- A day-by-day grid. Every habit has a colorful grid of your history. One empty square in a sea of color tells the real story far better than a zero. You can try it with the habit grid maker.

- Fill in a past day. Forgot to log yesterday's walk? Open the habit and tap the day to mark it done, or to log an amount for a number habit. Use this for days you actually did, not to rescue a streak.

- Weekly targets. For habits like "gym three times a week", the streak counts weeks, not days, so rest days are not misses. See weekly habit goals.

Habit Forever is free for up to three habits, with no account, and your habit data stays on your device. To check in faster so misses happen less often, add a widget: see how to add a habit tracker widget on iPhone.

## When a broken streak is a signal

Sometimes a run of misses is telling you something. If you keep missing the same habit, it may be too big, at the wrong time, or not something you really want. Shrink it, move it to a better cue, or archive it and keep its history while you focus on something else. Dropping a habit on purpose is a decision, not a failure.

If you prefer pen and paper for a fresh start, try our printable habit tracker.

## FAQ

Does missing one day ruin a habit?
No, research by Lally and colleagues found that missing a single opportunity did not materially affect the habit-forming process.

Should I start my habit over after missing a day?
You do not need to start over, because your earlier repetitions still count, so just do the habit again today.

Where does "never miss twice" come from?
It is a popular rule of thumb made widely known by James Clear's book Atomic Habits, and it is practical advice rather than a research finding.

Is it cheating to fill in a missed day in a habit app?
Filling in a day you actually did but forgot to log keeps your record accurate, while marking a day you did not do only hides useful information from yourself.

Is a streak or consistency the better measure?
Consistency gives a more honest long-term picture because one miss only dips it slightly, while a streak is useful for day-to-day motivation.

## Sources

- Lally P, van Jaarsveld CHM, Potts HWW, Wardle J. How are habits formed: Modelling habit formation in the real world. European Journal of Social Psychology, 2010.

# How to choose a private habit tracker with no account
URL: https://habitforever.app/guides/private-habit-tracker-no-account.html
Updated: 2026-10-22

Look for an app that works without sign-up, stores your habits on the device, and has a short App Store privacy label. Then check how it handles backup, because no account usually also means no cloud sync.

A private habit tracker is one that works without an account, keeps your habit records on your iPhone, and collects as little data as possible. You can check most of this before you download anything, from the App Store privacy label and the app's description.

Habits can be personal: drinking less, therapy homework, medication, spending. Here is how to judge an app's privacy honestly, including the trade-offs that come with keeping data on the device.

## 1. Read the App Store privacy label

Every App Store listing has an App Privacy section, filled in by the developer. Scroll down the app's page to find it. It groups data into a few categories:

- Data Not Collected: the developer says the app collects no data at all.

- Data Not Linked to You: some data is collected, but not tied to your identity.

- Data Linked to You: collected data is connected to your account, device or identity.

- Data Used to Track You: data is used to follow you across other companies' apps and websites, for example for advertising.

For a habit tracker, the most private result is "Data Not Collected". Many good apps show "Data Not Linked to You" because the services that process in-app purchases record purchase details and an anonymous identifier. That is normal for any app you can pay inside. A habit tracker that tracks you across other apps is a red flag.

Remember that the label is self-reported. It is a strong signal, not an audit.

## 2. Check whether an account is required

Many apps ask you to sign in on the first screen, often with Sign in with Apple, Google or an email address. An account is how most apps sync between devices, but it also means your habit list lives on someone's server.

Look for wording such as "no account", "no sign-up" or "works offline" in the description, or open the app and see whether you can create a habit straight away.

## 3. Understand the sync trade-off

There are three common approaches:

 | | Approach | Privacy | Trade-off

 | Developer's own server with an account | Your data is held by the developer | Easy sync across iPhone, Android and web

 | iCloud sync | Data stays in your iCloud, not the developer's server | Apple devices only

 | On device only | Data never leaves the device unless you export it | No automatic sync; you need your own backups

None of these is wrong. Decide which one you are comfortable with, and be suspicious of any app that is vague about it.

## 4. Make sure you can export your data

A private app should still let you take your data with you. Look for an export option, ideally in an open format such as JSON or CSV, and an import option to restore it. Without one, your history is stuck in the app forever, or lost with your phone.

## 5. Test it offline

Turn on Airplane Mode and try adding a check-in. A truly on-device app works exactly the same. If it complains or refuses, your data is going somewhere.

 

## Habit Forever, honestly

We make Habit Forever, so here is how it measures up against the checklist above, including where it falls short.

- No account. You open the app and start adding habits. There is no sign-up screen.

- On-device storage. Your habit records and notes are stored on your device. They are not sent to a server of ours.

- No iCloud sync. That is the trade-off: your habits do not sync between your iPhone and iPad automatically.

- Backup export and import. Habit Forever Pro can export a JSON backup of your habits and import it again, for example when you move to a new phone. The free plan does not include export.

- Privacy label. We do not claim "Data Not Collected". Purchases are handled by Apple and RevenueCat, so the label lists purchase information and identifiers, which are not linked to you.

- No ads. The app does not show ads.

Habit Forever is free for up to three habits, with goals, reminders and notes, and Pro has a one-time lifetime option (see habit trackers without a subscription). If you need habits synced across devices, an app with iCloud or account sync will suit you better; our comparison of the best habit tracker apps for iPhone shows which apps need an account. For questions about data, see our support page.

## The most private option of all

Paper. A printed grid on your desk has no privacy label because it needs none. If that appeals, use our printable habit tracker, or combine paper with an app for reminders.

## FAQ

Is there a habit tracker for iPhone that needs no account?
Yes, several habit trackers work without an account, including Habit Forever, Streaks and HabitKit.

Does a habit tracker without an account work offline?
Usually yes, because an app that stores habits on the device does not need a connection to log a check-in, and you can confirm this by testing it in Airplane Mode.

Does Habit Forever collect any data?
Habit Forever stores your habit records and notes on your device, and its App Store privacy label lists purchase information and identifiers that are not linked to you because purchases are handled by Apple and RevenueCat.

How do I move my habits to a new iPhone without an account?
Use the app's export feature to save a backup file and import it on the new phone; in Habit Forever this JSON export and import is part of Habit Forever Pro.

What does "Data Not Linked to You" mean?
It means the app collects some data, such as purchase details, but the developer states that it is not connected to your identity.

## Sources

- Apple Developer: App privacy details on the App Store

- Apple: Privacy labels

# How to track a habit you want to do less
URL: https://habitforever.app/guides/track-a-habit-you-want-to-do-less.html
Updated: 2026-11-18

To cut back on a habit, track a limit instead of a target: "at most 2 cups of coffee a day" or "under 2 hours of screen time", where every day you stay under counts as a win. Pair the limit with an if-then plan for the moment the old habit usually starts, and name what you will do instead.

Most habit trackers are built for doing more: more water, more steps, more pages. But a lot of what people want to change is about doing less. Coffee, scrolling, takeaway, impulse spending. A checklist with a tick for "did it" is the wrong shape for that, and I built limits into Habit Forever for exactly this reason. This guide covers the built-in tools first, then what the research says about breaking a habit, then how to track it.

A note before we start: this is about everyday habits. If you are trying to stop drinking, smoking, gambling or using a drug, or a habit feels out of your control, please talk to a doctor or a support service. A tracker can sit alongside that help, but it is not treatment. In the UK, the NHS addiction support page lists where to start.

## Built-in tools on iPhone

Screen time is the one habit iPhone measures for you. Screen Time in Settings shows your daily average and how often you pick up your phone, and Time Allowances (App Limits on older iOS versions) let you set a daily budget for app categories such as social media or games. If screen time is your target, set that up first: it measures automatically, which no tracker can match.

For most other habits, coffee, sweets, spending, there is nothing built in that counts them. A tally in the Notes app or on paper works: one mark per cup, and a line under the day when you stayed under your limit. Our printable habit tracker gives you a monthly grid for that, and the habit cost calculator shows what a habit costs you in a year.

## What research says about breaking a habit

Habits are triggered by situations: the same time, place, mood or preceding action. That is why willpower alone tends to lose. Two ideas from the research are worth using.

If-then plans. The psychologist Peter Gollwitzer called them implementation intentions: a plan in the form "if situation Y happens, then I will do Z". His 1999 paper in American Psychologist described how linking a specific situation to a specific response helps people act on their goals, and a 2006 meta-analysis with Paschal Sheeran found a positive effect across 94 independent tests. A 2024 review of 642 tests by Sheeran, Listrom and Gollwitzer found the effects were larger when plans used the if-then format and when people were highly motivated to reach the goal. It is a helpful tool, not a guarantee.

Name a replacement. In three experiments, Marieke Adriaanse, Gollwitzer and colleagues (2011) studied if-then plans that replace a habitual response with an alternative one in a critical situation, such as a snack habit. The plans removed the old habit's head start in the mind, but people only changed what they did when they also strongly wanted the alternative. In practice: pick a replacement you actually like.

Put together, a good plan sounds like: "If I want a third coffee after lunch, then I will make a herbal tea." Or: "If I pick up my phone in bed, then I will put it on the charger across the room."

## Set a limit, not zero (usually)

Going from four coffees to none is hard, and one slip can feel like total failure. Going from four to two is a goal you can hit tomorrow. A limit also keeps the habit honest: you still see exactly how much you had, so the trend is visible even on a day you went over.

- Daily limits suit habits that happen most days: coffee, screen time, sweets, daily spending.

- Weekly limits suit habits that are fine now and then: takeaway meals, nights out, hours of gaming. A weekly limit leaves you free to choose the day.

- A clean break suits a habit you want gone completely. Track the days without it rather than the slips.

 

## How to track a limit in Habit Forever

- Add a new habit, for example "Coffee".

- Under Goal, choose Stay under.

- Set the number and unit, such as at most 2 cups, and choose Each day or Each week.

- Turn on One tap adds with 1, so each cup is a single tap on the habit's circle.

The new habit list has a "Do less of" group with ready-made ideas: screen time under 2 hours a day, coffee under 2 cups, daily spending under a limit in your currency, and "No sweets", a check-off habit for a day without.

Here is how a limit counts:

- Entries add up. Log each cup or each purchase as it happens; the day's total is what counts.

- A day with nothing logged counts as zero, so it is a success. You do not have to open the app to record "none today".

- Going over shows as over, and that day breaks the streak. Your streak is the run of days (or weeks) you stayed at or under the limit.

- The history stays honest. The day-by-day grid fills in the days you stayed under, and the number you logged is kept, so you can see a week of 3 cups become a week of 2.

For a clean break, either set a limit of 0, so every day with nothing logged counts, or use a check-off habit that you tick for each day without. You can add a note to any check-in, which is a good place for what triggered a slip and what you will try next time.

Reminders help here in a different way: set one for the time the urge usually hits, such as 3 pm for the afternoon coffee, as a prompt to use your if-then plan. Pro adds patterns such as your strongest days of the week, which can show when a limit is easiest and hardest to keep.

## After a slip

A day over the limit is information, not a verdict. Look at what happened (the time, the place, how you felt), adjust the if-then plan, and keep the limit for tomorrow. If you keep going over by a lot, the limit may be too ambitious for now: raise it a little, hold it for a few weeks, then lower it again. Read what to do when you break a streak for more on recovering from a bad day.

Cutting back also works best with something new in its place. If you want to stack a good habit onto an existing moment, see habit stacking.

## FAQ

How do I track a habit I want to stop?
Track a limit instead of a target, such as at most 2 cups of coffee a day, or for a clean break, track the days without it rather than the slips.

Do I have to log days when I did not do the habit?
No, in Habit Forever a day with nothing logged counts as zero, so it counts as a success for a limit.

What is an if-then plan?
An if-then plan, which researchers call an implementation intention, links a specific situation to a specific response, such as "if I want a third coffee after lunch, then I will make a herbal tea".

Can a habit tracker help with addiction?
A tracker is not treatment; if a habit involves alcohol, smoking, gambling or drugs, or feels out of your control, talk to a doctor or a support service.

## Sources

- Gollwitzer, P. M. (1999). Implementation intentions: Strong effects of simple plans. American Psychologist, 54(7), 493–503.

- Gollwitzer, P. M., & Sheeran, P. (2006). Implementation intentions and goal achievement: A meta-analysis of effects and processes. Advances in Experimental Social Psychology, 38, 69–119.

- Adriaanse, M. A., Gollwitzer, P. M., De Ridder, D. T. D., de Wit, J. B. F., & Kroese, F. M. (2011). Breaking habits with implementation intentions: A test of underlying processes. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 37(4), 502–513.

- Sheeran, P., Listrom, O., & Gollwitzer, P. M. (2024). The when and how of planning: Meta-analysis of the scope and components of implementation intentions in 642 tests. European Review of Social Psychology.

- Apple Support: Set up Screen Time for yourself on iPhone

- NHS: Addiction support

# How to track water intake on iPhone
URL: https://habitforever.app/guides/track-water-intake-iphone.html
Updated: 2026-10-22

The built-in way is the Health app: find Water under Nutrition and tap Add Data. If you want a daily goal, a streak and one-tap logging from a widget, track water as a number habit in a habit tracker instead.

To track water intake on iPhone without installing anything, open the Health app, find Water in the Nutrition category, and tap Add Data to log each drink. If you would rather count glasses toward a daily goal and keep a streak, a habit tracker with number habits is quicker day to day.

Here are both methods, step by step, with the honest pros and cons of each.

## Method 1: Log water in the Apple Health app

The Health app comes with every iPhone and has a Water data type in its Nutrition category.

- Open the Health app.

- Go to Browse. On iOS 17 and 18 it is a tab at the bottom of the screen; on newer versions, use the browse or search button at the bottom right.

- Tap Nutrition, then tap Water. You can also simply search for "Water".

- Tap Add Data in the top-right corner.

- Enter the amount, check the date and time, and tap Add.

To see your water on the Summary screen every day, scroll down on the Water page and tap Pin to Summary. You can change the unit (for example milliliters or fluid ounces) under Unit on the same page.

### Pros and cons of the Health app

- Pros: free and built in; charts by day, week, month and year; other apps you allow can add water data too.

- Cons: logging takes several taps every time; there is no daily goal to hit, no streak, and no reminder to drink.

The Health app is a good record. It is not designed to help you build the habit of drinking more.

## Why track water as a habit instead

Most people who want to track water really want to drink more water, consistently. That is a habit problem, and habit tools help with it:

- A daily target, such as 8 glasses, so you know when you are done.

- One-tap logging from the Home Screen or Lock Screen, so a glass takes one second to record.

- Reminders at times that suit you, which stop once you have hit the target.

- A streak and a grid, so a good week is visible and worth protecting.

 

## Method 2: Track water in Habit Forever

We make Habit Forever, a habit tracker for iPhone and iPad. Water is one of its starter habits, so setup takes seconds.

- Tap to add a habit and choose Drink water from the suggestions. It starts as 8 glasses a day, with one tap adding one glass.

- Or build your own: pick Reach a number as the goal, set the amount (for example 8) and the unit (glasses, ml, or anything you like).

- Set the amount a single tap adds, such as one glass, so tapping the habit logs it instantly.

- Add a reminder or two, for example mid-morning and mid-afternoon. Reminders only arrive on the habit's days and never once it is done.

### Log a glass in one tap

- In the app: tap the habit to add a glass, or open it to type a different amount.

- From a widget: add the Habit widget to your Home Screen or Lock Screen and tap its check-in button to check in without opening the app; for a number habit, a tap logs your one-tap amount. To add several glasses in a row, use the app or Siri. See how to add a habit tracker widget.

- With Siri or Shortcuts: the "Check In Habit" action accepts an optional amount and note, so you can log 2 glasses by voice or build a Shortcut for your water bottle. See how to log habits with Siri and Shortcuts.

### See your progress

Each habit shows your current and best streak, your consistency, and a colorful day-by-day grid. Habit Forever Pro adds deeper insights, such as your best days and time of day.

One thing to know: Habit Forever does not connect to Apple Health. Water you log in the app is not written to Health, and water logged in Health does not appear in the app. If you need your water in Health, for example for a nutrition app that reads it, use Method 1 as well, or choose an app that writes to Health.

## Which method is right for you?

 | | | Health app | Habit tracker

 | Daily goal | No | Yes

 | Streak and grid | No | Yes

 | One-tap widget | No | Yes

 | Reminders | No | Yes

 | Shared with other health apps | Yes | Habit Forever: no

## Tips for drinking more water

- Tie it to a cue. A glass after waking, with each meal and after brushing your teeth already gets you to four.

- Use the same glass or bottle so your unit means something.

- Start below your goal. If you drink 3 glasses now, aim for 5 before 8.

- Ask a professional about your needs. How much water you need depends on your body, activity and climate. For a starting number from official guidance, try the water intake calculator.

For more on making it stick, read how long it takes to form a habit.

## FAQ

Does iPhone have a built-in water tracker?
Yes, the Health app has a Water data type under Nutrition where you can tap Add Data to log each drink, although it has no daily goal or reminders.

Can I log water from my iPhone Lock Screen?
Yes, with a habit tracker that has interactive Lock Screen widgets, such as Habit Forever, you can check in on your water habit from the widget without opening the app, and log extra glasses in the app or with Siri.

Does Habit Forever sync water with Apple Health?
No, Habit Forever does not integrate with Apple Health, so water logged in the app stays in the app.

Can I log water with Siri?
Yes, Habit Forever's Check In Habit action for Siri and Shortcuts accepts an optional amount, so you can log more than one glass at a time.

Can I track water in milliliters instead of glasses?
Yes, in Habit Forever you can set any unit for a number habit, including milliliters or ounces.

## Sources

- Apple Support: View your data in Health on iPhone

- Apple Support: Intro to Health data on iPhone

# How to track a "3 times a week" habit
URL: https://habitforever.app/guides/weekly-habit-goals.html
Updated: 2026-11-18

To track a habit you want to do 3 times a week, give it a weekly goal instead of a daily one: the week counts as done once you reach 3, on whichever days suit you, and the streak counts weeks. If your days are fixed, such as Monday, Wednesday and Friday, schedule only those days so the others never count as misses.

The gym, a long run, calling your parents, cooking at home: plenty of good habits are not daily. Track them with a daily checklist and every rest day looks like a failure, and the streak resets for no reason. A weekly goal fixes that. Here is how to set one up with what is already on your iPhone, and then how Habit Forever counts it.

## First, decide which kind of weekly habit it is

- Fixed days. You run on Monday, Wednesday and Friday. The habit belongs to those days.

- Flexible days. You want three workouts a week, whenever they fit. Tuesday, Saturday and Sunday counts just as well.

Flexible goals are kinder to a busy life, because a missed Monday can still be made up on Thursday. Fixed days are easier to plan around and to attach reminders to. Neither is better; pick the one that matches how your week really goes.

## With built-in apps

Reminders handles fixed days well. Create a reminder such as "Run", open its details, set a time and choose a custom repeat on the weekdays you want. It comes back on those days and you tick it off. What it cannot do is flexible days: there is no way to say "any three days this week", and it keeps no count of how many weeks you managed.

Paper handles flexible days well. Draw one row per week and make a tally mark each time you go; three marks and the week is done. Our printable habit tracker works for this if you treat each row as a week. What paper cannot do is remind you on Thursday that you still have two to go.

## Flexible days in Habit Forever: a weekly goal

I built weekly goals into Habit Forever because "3 times a week" is one of the most natural goals there is. To set one up:

- Tap to add a new habit and give it a name, such as "Run".

- Under Goal, choose Reach a number.

- Set it to at least 3, type or pick a unit such as "times" or "runs", and choose Each week.

- Turn on One tap adds and set it to 1, so each tap of the habit's circle logs one session without a keypad.

There is also a ready-made "Run: 3 runs a week" idea in the new habit list that fills all of this in for you.

During the week, the habit shows how far along you are this week. Once you reach 3, the week counts as done, however the sessions were spread.

### How the streak counts

For a habit with a weekly goal, the streak is counted in weeks, not days. Each week in which you reached your goal adds one; a week in which you fell short ends the streak. A few details matter:

- The current week is never held against you. On Wednesday with one session logged, your streak is not broken; the week is not over yet. Only a finished week that fell short breaks it.

- You choose when a week starts. In Settings, "Week starts on" can be Monday, Sunday or Saturday, and the weekly count follows it.

- The best streak is in weeks too, and the consistency figure becomes the share of recent weeks in which you reached the goal.

- On the day-by-day grid, a week you completed is filled in as a whole week, so a run of good weeks reads as one solid band of color. You can draw a grid like this for any habit with the free habit grid maker.

Siri tells you the same thing: ask "What's my streak in Habit Forever" and the answer comes in weeks. See how to log habits with Siri and Shortcuts.

 

## Fixed days in Habit Forever: a schedule

If your habit belongs to specific days, keep it a simple check-off habit and change its Days from Every day to Weekdays, or tap Choose and pick the days. On the other days the habit shows as a rest day. As the app puts it: days off never break a streak. A Monday, Wednesday, Friday habit with all three done this week and last week is a streak of six, not a broken chain.

Reminders follow the habit's days too, and stay quiet once you have checked in.

## Weekly limits for things you want less of

A weekly goal also works as a limit. "Stay under" with "Each week" suits habits that are fine in moderation but add up: takeaway meals, hours of gaming, money spent on a hobby. The week counts as a success as long as your total stays at or under the limit. See how to track a habit you want to do less for more on limits.

New habits in Habit Forever take a daily or a weekly goal, not a monthly one. For something you do about once a month, such as paying a bill or a deep clean, a monthly repeating reminder in the Reminders app is the simpler tool.

## Tips for a weekly habit that lasts

- Set the goal you can hit in a bad week. If you sometimes manage four workouts and sometimes two, set three, or even two. A streak of hit weeks is worth more than an ambitious goal you miss half the time.

- Plan your days on Sunday. A flexible goal still needs a plan; decide which days you will aim for, and treat the others as back-ups.

- Do not save it all for the weekend. If the week is half gone and you have done none, do a short session today rather than hoping for three on Saturday.

- Expect it to take time. Automaticity grows with repetitions, so a weekly habit usually takes longer to feel automatic than a daily one; see how long it takes to form a habit.

Missed a week? It happens. Read what to do after a missed day; the same advice applies to a missed week.

## FAQ

How do I track a habit 3 times a week?
Give it a weekly goal of 3 so the week counts as done once you reach 3 on any days, or, if your days are fixed, schedule the habit only on those days.

Does a weekly habit break my streak on rest days?
No, in Habit Forever a habit with a weekly goal counts its streak in weeks, and the current week is never held against you until it ends.

Can I choose which day my week starts on?
Yes, in Habit Forever's Settings, "Week starts on" can be Monday, Sunday or Saturday, and weekly goals follow it.

Can the Reminders app track a 3 times a week habit?
Reminders can repeat on fixed weekdays, but it cannot count "any three days this week" or show how many weeks you managed.

## Sources

- Apple Support: Create reminders on iPhone

- Habit Forever on the App Store

Track check-off or number habits with goals, reminders, notes, streaks and colorful day-by-day grids, plus Home Screen and Lock Screen widgets and Siri Shortcuts. There is no account, and habit data stays on your device. It is free for up to three habits; Habit Forever Pro (yearly, monthly or a one-time lifetime purchase) adds unlimited habits, deeper insights, widgets for every habit and backup export/import. It is rated 4.6★ on the App Store, from 17 ratings worldwide, where it is listed as “Habit Forever: Streak Tracker” (formerly “Habit Streak Tracker: Routines”).

## What it does

 
- Two kinds of habit. Check-off habits (done or not), or number habits counted in pages, glasses, minutes, distance, money or a unit you name.
 
- Four kinds of goal. Check it off, reach a number (8 glasses, 20 pages), stay under a limit for things you want less of (2 hours, 2 coffees), or just track a reading such as weight or mood. Goals are per day or per week, on every day, weekdays or chosen days, and days off never break a streak.
 
- Progress you can see. Current and best streak, a consistency figure, and a colorful day-by-day grid for each habit, similar to a GitHub contribution graph. Milestone celebrations.
 
- Three Today layouts. Grid, Board (months of days for each habit) and Week.
 
- Reminders for each habit that stay quiet on days you’ve already checked in.
 
- Notes on any check-in, and you can fill in a missed day from the last seven days. Archive a habit and keep its history.
 
- Widgets on the Home Screen and Lock Screen that let you check in without opening the app.
 
- Siri and Shortcuts: Check In Habit (with an optional amount and note), Get Habit Streak and Open Habit.
 
- Light and dark themes, Dynamic Type and VoiceOver.

Free includes up to three habits with check-off and number habits, goals and limits, reminders, notes, streaks and grids, and a widget for your first habit. Pro adds unlimited habits, deeper insights (best days, time of day, month by month), widgets for every habit and backup export and import.

## What it doesn’t do

To keep descriptions accurate: Habit Forever has no Apple Watch app, no Apple Health integration, no iCloud sync, no Android, Mac or web version, no social features or challenges, and no AI features. If someone needs those, our comparison says which app fits better.

# Privacy policy
URL: https://habitforever.app/privacy.html
Updated: 2026-10-22

Short version: no account, no ads, no tracking. Your habits, check-ins and notes stay on your device. Purchases go through Apple and RevenueCat.

Effective date: October 22, 2026. This policy covers the Habit Forever app for iPhone and iPad (“Habit Forever: Streak Tracker” on the App Store, formerly “Habit Streak Tracker: Routines”) and this website. The developer and data controller is Mohamed Elatabany (“I”). Contact: atabany.apps@gmail.com.

## Your habit data stays on your device

Habits, check-ins, amounts, notes, reminders and settings are stored only on your device. There is no account, and I don’t operate a server that receives them. The app doesn’t sync them through iCloud. Home Screen and Lock Screen widgets, Siri and Shortcuts read the same on-device data. Reminders are scheduled as local notifications on your device.

If you use backup export (Pro), the app creates a file and you decide where it goes. I never receive it unless you send it to me.

## Purchases

Payments are processed by Apple; I never see your payment details. The app uses RevenueCat to manage subscriptions and the lifetime purchase. To do that, RevenueCat receives purchase information (such as the product, transaction and its status) together with an anonymous app user ID generated by the app, along with basic device information such as the app version and operating system. This information isn’t linked to your name or email, and it isn’t used for advertising. It appears in the App Store privacy label as Purchases and Identifiers, “not linked to you”.

## No tracking, no ads, no analytics

The app contains no advertising, no third-party analytics and no tracking across apps or websites. It doesn’t request your location, contacts or photos.

## Support emails

If you email me, I receive your email address and whatever you include, and use it only to reply. You can ask me to delete our correspondence at any time.

## This website

This site is static and hosted on GitHub Pages. It sets no cookies and runs no analytics or ads. The hosting provider may keep standard server logs, such as IP addresses, for security. The free tools run entirely in your browser and send nothing anywhere. Links to the App Store include a campaign tag so Apple can tell me, in aggregate, which page a download came from; Apple does not share personal data with me.

## Your choices and rights

 
- Delete any habit or entry in the app, or delete the app to remove all its data from the device.
 
- Export your data (Pro) whenever you like.
 
- Depending on where you live (for example under the GDPR or the CCPA), you may have rights to access, correct, delete or port personal data. Because I hold almost nothing about you, most requests are answered by the controls above; for anything else, email me.

## Children

The app isn’t directed to children under 13, and I don’t knowingly collect personal information from them.

## Changes

If this policy changes, I’ll update the effective date above and describe significant changes in the app’s release notes.

# Support
URL: https://habitforever.app/support.html
Updated: 2026-10-22

Answers to the most common questions, and a direct line to the developer. I read every email.

## Contact

Email atabany.apps@gmail.com. You can also tap Contact support in the app’s Settings. It helps to mention your iPhone model and iOS version. I usually reply within two working days.

## Purchases and subscriptions

How do I restore Habit Forever Pro on a new iPhone?
Sign in with the same Apple Account you bought Pro with, open the app, open the Pro screen and tap Restore. Your subscription or lifetime purchase is linked to your Apple Account, not to the device.

How do I cancel my subscription?
Open the Settings app on your iPhone, tap your name, then Subscriptions, choose Habit Forever and tap Cancel Subscription. You keep Pro until the end of the period you paid for. Deleting the app doesn’t cancel a subscription.

How do I request a refund?
Purchases are made through Apple, so refunds are handled by Apple at reportaproblem.apple.com. Sign in, choose the purchase and select Request a refund.

## Your data

Where are my habits stored?
On your device. Habit Forever has no account and no server copy of your habits, check-ins or notes, and it doesn’t sync through iCloud.

How do I move my habits to a new iPhone?
With Pro, open Settings in the app and tap Export backup. Send the file to your new device (AirDrop, Files or email), then tap Import backup in the same Settings screen. A full device-to-device iPhone transfer or an encrypted iPhone backup also carries the app’s data.

I deleted the app. Can I get my habits back?
Only from a backup. Deleting the app removes its data from the device. If you exported a backup or have an iPhone backup from before the deletion, you can restore from it.

## Reminders and widgets

My reminders don’t arrive.
Check Settings → Notifications → Habit Forever and make sure Allow Notifications is on. Then check that a Focus mode isn’t silencing the app, and that the habit’s reminder is set for the days you expect.

How do I add a widget?
Touch and hold an empty area of the Home Screen, tap Edit, then Add Widget, and search for Habit Forever. For the Lock Screen, touch and hold the Lock Screen, tap Customize, choose the Lock Screen and tap the widget area. The guide to habit tracker widgets has step-by-step instructions.

More detail: habit tracker widgets on iPhone.

## Is this the app formerly called Habit Tracker?

Yes. Before version 4.0 it was listed as “Habit Streak Tracker: Routines” and showed “Habit Tracker” on the Home Screen. Updating keeps all your habits and history.

# Habit cost calculator
URL: https://habitforever.app/tools/habit-cost-calculator.html
Updated: 2026-11-18

A habit that costs 5 a day costs 1,825 a year and 18,250 over ten years, in whatever currency you pay; an hour a day of scrolling adds up to 365 hours a year, about 15 full days. Enter your own habit to see its cost in money and time, and what cutting back would save.

Habit

 CHFSEKNOKDKKPLNTRY

 Cut back by 50%
 
 
 
 
 Enter a cost and how often. Everything is calculated in your browser; nothing is sent anywhere or saved.

 
 The calculator needs JavaScript. The tables below have the totals for common amounts.

## What a habit costs over time

Amounts are in your own currency: a habit that costs 5 a day costs the same multiple whether that is dollars, euros, pounds or dirhams. A year is 365 days and a month is a twelfth of a year.

 | | Cost a day | A week | A month | A year | 10 years

 
 | 1 | 7 | 30.42 | 365 | 3,650

 | 2 | 14 | 60.83 | 730 | 7,300

 | 3 | 21 | 91.25 | 1,095 | 10,950

 | 4.50 | 31.50 | 136.88 | 1,642.50 | 16,425

 | 5 | 35 | 152.08 | 1,825 | 18,250

 | 10 | 70 | 304.17 | 3,650 | 36,500

 | 15 | 105 | 456.25 | 5,475 | 54,750

 | 20 | 140 | 608.33 | 7,300 | 73,000

 

## What a habit costs in time

Time is the cost people forget. “Waking days” assumes 16 waking hours a day.

 | | Time a day | Hours a year | Full days a year | Waking days a year

 
 | 15 minutes | 91 | 3.8 | 5.7

 | 30 minutes | 183 | 7.6 | 11.4

 | 1 hour | 365 | 15.2 | 22.8

 | 2 hours | 730 | 30.4 | 45.6

 | 3 hours | 1,095 | 45.6 | 68.4

 | 4 hours | 1,460 | 60.8 | 91.2

 

## How it works

 
- Times a year = how many times × 365 for a day, × 365 ÷ 7 for a week, × 12 for a month, or × 1 for a year.
 
- Cost a year = cost each time × times a year. A week is that ÷ (365 ÷ 7), a month ÷ 12, and 10 years × 10.
 
- Time a year = minutes each time × times a year ÷ 60, in hours; ÷ 24 for full days, ÷ 16 for waking days.
 
- Cutting back by X% saves X% of each figure, because the cost scales with how often you do it.

It’s simple arithmetic on purpose. It ignores price rises, and it doesn’t add interest you might earn by saving the money instead, so long-run totals are, if anything, on the low side.

## Cutting back without quitting

You don’t have to quit to save. A habit you do half as often costs half as much, and a limit you can keep, such as “two coffees a day” or “no more than 30 minutes of social media”, often lasts longer than an all-or-nothing rule. Pick a number a little below what you do now, count it every day, and lower it once it feels easy. My guide on tracking a habit you want to do less goes into how. If you slip one day, carry on the next; a single miss doesn’t undo the habit, as I explain in what a broken streak really means.

 

## FAQ

How much does a coffee a day cost a year?
Multiply the price by 365. At 5 a cup in your currency, one coffee a day is 1,825 a year and 18,250 over ten years. Two a day doubles it.

How much time does an hour of scrolling a day add up to?
365 hours a year, which is about 15 full days or nearly 23 waking days of 16 hours.

Does the calculator include inflation or interest?
No. It multiplies today’s cost by how often you pay it, so real long-run totals are usually higher.

Is my data saved?
No. The numbers stay in your browser; nothing is uploaded or stored.

# How long until it’s a habit? Calculator
URL: https://habitforever.app/tools/habit-formation-calculator.html
Updated: 2026-10-22

Enter the day you started. The calculator shows where you are against what research has measured: a median of 66 days to reach near-peak automaticity, with a range of 18 to 254 days.

I started my habit on
 
 
 
 Habit (optional)
 
 
 
 
 Pick a start date to see your timeline. Everything is calculated in your browser; nothing is sent anywhere.

 
 The calculator needs JavaScript. The reference table below has the same milestones.

## The milestones, from the research

These figures come from two studies. Lally and colleagues (2010) followed 96 volunteers who each chose a new daily eating, drinking or exercise habit in the same context, such as after breakfast. Singh and colleagues (2024) pooled 20 studies with 2,601 participants. “Automatic” here means the behavior feels like something you do without thinking; it doesn’t mean the habit is finished.

 | | Day | What it means | Source

 
 | 18 | Fastest time to reach 95% of the automaticity plateau | Lally et al., 2010

 | 59–66 | Median times across the studies in the 2024 review | Singh et al., 2024

 | 66 | Median time to reach 95% of the plateau (39 people with a good model fit) | Lally et al., 2010

 | 84 | End of the daily reporting period; later values were extrapolated | Lally et al., 2010

 | 106–154 | Mean (average) times in the 2024 review; a few slow habits pull the average up | Singh et al., 2024

 | 254 | Slowest estimated time to reach the plateau | Lally et al., 2010

 | 335 | Longest time reported across the review | Singh et al., 2024

 

## How to read your result

The median is the middle person, not a deadline. Half of the people in Lally’s study took longer than 66 days, and the time varied widely between people and between behaviors, from a glass of water to a daily run. If you’re past day 66 and it still takes effort, you’re not behind. You’re in the normal range.

Missing a day is normal too. In the same study, missing one opportunity did not materially affect how the habit formed. What mattered was repeating the behavior in a consistent context. That’s why a grid of days is more useful than a streak counter alone: it shows the pattern, not just the last break. More on that in what to do when you miss a day.

The bigger story behind these numbers, including where the “21 days” idea came from, is in How long does it take to form a habit?

 

## FAQ

Is it 21 days or 66 days to form a habit?
The best-known measurement found a median of 66 days to reach near-peak automaticity, with a range of 18 to 254 days. The 21-day figure is a popular rule of thumb rather than a measured result for forming habits.

Does the calculator store my data?
No. The calculation runs in your browser and nothing is sent to a server or saved.

Does missing a day reset the clock?
No. In Lally and colleagues’ 2010 study, missing one opportunity did not materially affect the habit formation process. Keep going the next day.

Why is the range so wide?
People, habits and situations differ. Participants chose very different behaviors, from drinking water to exercising, and some never reached a clear plateau during the 84 days they were tracked.

## Sources

 
- Lally, P., van Jaarsveld, C. H. M., Potts, H. W. W., & Wardle, J. (2010). How are habits formed: Modelling habit formation in the real world. European Journal of Social Psychology, 40(6), 998–1009. doi.org/10.1002/ejsp.674
 
- Singh, B., Murphy, A., Maher, C., & Smith, A. E. (2024). Time to form a habit: a systematic review and meta-analysis of health behaviour habit formation and its determinants. Healthcare, 12(23), 2488. doi.org/10.3390/healthcare12232488

# Habit grid maker
URL: https://habitforever.app/tools/habit-grid-maker.html
Updated: 2026-11-18

Type a habit, pick a colour, then tap or drag across the days you did it, or fill them from a start date with a done rate. You get a year of colored squares, like a GitHub contribution graph, with your streaks counted, ready to download as a PNG.

Habit name

 Tap a square to switch a day on or off, or drag across squares with a mouse. With a keyboard, use the arrow keys to move and Space to switch a day.

 
 The grid maker needs JavaScript to draw your squares.

 
 
 Download PNG

 The grid maker needs JavaScript. Nothing you make is uploaded; the image is drawn in your browser.

## How full a year of squares gets

A done rate turns into squares like this. A year has 365 squares (366 in a leap year), arranged in 52 or 53 columns of weeks.

 | | Done rate | Squares filled in a year | In a 30-day month | Days a week, on average

 
 | 100% | 365 | 30 | 7

 | 90% | 329 | 27 | 6.3

 | 80% | 292 | 24 | 5.6

 | 70% | 256 | 21 | 4.9

 | 50% | 183 | 15 | 3.5

 | 3 days a week | 156 | 13 | 3

 

## How it works

 
- Columns are weeks, rows are weekdays. The first column starts on the Monday (or Sunday) on or before the first day of the range, so a year needs 53 columns.
 
- Fill automatically switches on about the chosen share of days from the start date to today, at random but repeatably, so the same settings give the same grid. Days before the start date stay empty.
 
- Streaks. The current streak counts back from today, or from yesterday if today isn’t marked yet. The best streak is the longest unbroken run. Consistency is days done ÷ days so far in the range.
 
- The PNG is drawn on a canvas in your browser at double resolution, with the habit name, the counts and a small habitforever.app credit. Nothing is uploaded.

## Why a grid beats a streak counter

A streak number only tells you about the last break. A grid shows the whole pattern: the strong months, the weekend gaps, the week you were ill and came straight back. That matters, because missing a single day didn’t materially affect habit formation in Lally and colleagues’ 2010 study. One empty square in a long run of color looks like what it is, a blip. More on that in what a broken streak really means, and how long the squares usually take to add up to a habit in how long it takes to form a habit.

 

## FAQ

What is a habit grid?
A habit grid shows one square per day, colored when you did the habit, laid out in columns of weeks like a GitHub contribution graph. It makes a year of consistency visible at a glance.

Can I make a grid for a past year?
Yes. Choose a year in the Range menu, then tap the days you did it or fill them from a start date with a done rate.

Is anything I make uploaded?
No. The grid and the PNG are made in your browser, and nothing is sent to a server or saved.

Can I use the image anywhere?
Yes. The PNG is yours to share or print. It carries a small habitforever.app credit in the corner.

 Fill a square each day you do it. Made with the free printable at habitforever.app

 

## How to use a paper habit tracker

 
- Keep the list short. Three to six habits is plenty. A sheet full of empty rows is discouraging; a short list you mostly fill is motivating.
 
- Make each habit specific. “Read 10 pages” is easier to mark than “read more”. If a habit has a number, put it in the name.
 
- Mark it right after you do it. Keep the sheet where the habit happens: on the fridge for water, by the bed for reading.
 
- Missed a day? Leave it blank and carry on. One gap doesn’t undo your progress. Research on habit formation found that missing a single day didn’t materially affect it. See what to do when you break a streak.
 
- Look at the month as a whole. At the end, count the filled squares per row. That number, your consistency, says more than your longest streak.

## Paper or an app?

Paper is great when the sheet sits where you’ll see it. It falls short when you’re away from home, when you want reminders, or when a habit is a number you’d like totals for. If you want the same grid of days on your iPhone, with reminders, widgets and streaks counted for you, that’s what Habit Forever does. Our guide on how to track habits on iPhone compares the options, including the free built-in ones.

 

## FAQ

Is this printable habit tracker free?
Yes. It is free with no sign-up. Print as many sheets as you like or save them as PDFs.

How do I save the habit tracker as a PDF?
Select Print or save as PDF, then choose Save as PDF as the destination in your browser’s print dialog. On iPhone, tap Print, then use the share button in the print preview to save it to Files.

How many habits fit on one page?
Up to 12 habits fit on one landscape page with a column for every day of the month.

Is my habit list uploaded anywhere?
No. The sheet is built in your browser and nothing is sent to a server or stored.

 | 30 | 26.0 | 31.6

 | 45 | 38.9 | 47.4

 | 60 | 51.9 | 63.2

 

## How it works

 
- Reading days = days from the start date to the finish date, counting both, × days you read each week ÷ 7.
 
- Pages a day = books × pages per book ÷ reading days.
 
- Minutes a day = pages a day × words per page ÷ words a minute.

The 300 pages per book and 275 words per page are my assumptions, not measured averages: books vary a lot, so change them to match what you read. A dense paperback can hold far more words on a page than a large-print or illustrated book. The reading speed comes from research: Marc Brysbaert’s 2019 meta-analysis of 190 studies with 18,573 participants put adult silent reading in English at 238 words a minute for non-fiction and 260 for fiction. The often-quoted 300 words a minute is higher than what most people read.

## Make the goal a daily habit

A yearly number is easy to set and easy to forget. A small daily number is the one you can act on tonight: 10 pages before bed is a book a month. Tie it to something you already do, like after dinner or on the train, and count pages rather than books, so a slow week with a long book still shows progress. More ideas in how to build a reading habit. If you miss a day, carry on the next; one gap doesn’t undo a habit, as I explain in what a broken streak really means.

 

## FAQ

How many pages a day do I need to read 52 books a year?
About 43 pages a day, or roughly 49 minutes at 238 words a minute, if your books average 300 pages with 275 words a page. Shorter books or a faster reading speed bring that down.

How many pages a day is 12 books a year?
About 10 pages a day, roughly 11 minutes, with 300-page books. That is one book a month.

What is the average reading speed?
Brysbaert’s 2019 review of 190 studies found that adults read English silently at about 238 words a minute for non-fiction and 260 for fiction. Your own speed depends on the text and why you’re reading it.

Do audiobooks count?
That’s your call. In the calculator, set the reading speed to the narrator’s pace instead, or track minutes rather than pages.

## Sources

 
- Brysbaert, M. (2019). How many words do we read per minute? A review and meta-analysis of reading rate. Journal of Memory and Language, 109, 104047. doi.org/10.1016/j.jml.2019.104047

# How much water should I drink a day?
URL: https://habitforever.app/tools/water-intake-calculator.html
Updated: 2026-11-18

The US National Academies set an adequate intake of about 2.7 litres of total water a day for women and 3.7 litres for men, and about 80% of it usually comes from drinks: roughly 2.2 L (9 cups) for women and 3.0 L (13 cups) for men. The calculator adds what exercise and heat take out and turns it into glasses.

 Choose your options to see a daily number. Everything is calculated in your browser; nothing is sent anywhere or saved.

 
 The calculator needs JavaScript. The tables below have the same numbers for a sedentary day in a mild climate.

This is a starting point for healthy adults, not medical advice. Thirst is a good guide for most people: the National Academies panel wrote that “the vast majority of healthy people adequately meet their daily hydration needs by letting thirst be their guide.” If you have a health condition, read when to ask a doctor first.

## Daily water by guideline

These are adequate intakes for a sedentary day in a temperate climate. “Total water” includes the water in food; “from drinks” counts every drink, including tea, coffee and milk. Cups are 8 US fl oz (237 mL).

 US National Academies adequate intakes for water
 | | US National Academies | Total water | From drinks | US fl oz from drinks | 250 mL glasses | 8 oz cups

 
 | Women, 19+ | 2.7 L | 2.2 L | 74 | 8.8 | 9.3

 | Men, 19+ | 3.7 L | 3.0 L | 101 | 12 | 12.7

 | Pregnant | 3.0 L | 2.3 L | 78 | 9.2 | 9.7

 | Breastfeeding | 3.8 L | 3.1 L | 105 | 12.4 | 13.1

 

The European Food Safety Authority set lower values. EFSA gives total water only; the “from drinks” column assumes about 80% comes from drinks, the share the National Academies observed, so treat it as an estimate.

 EFSA adequate intakes for water
 | | EFSA | Total water | From drinks (est.) | US fl oz from drinks | 250 mL glasses | 8 oz cups

 
 | Women, adults | 2.0 L | 1.6 L | 54 | 6.4 | 6.8

 | Men, adults | 2.5 L | 2.0 L | 68 | 8 | 8.5

 | Pregnant | 2.3 L | 1.84 L | 62 | 7.4 | 7.8

 | Breastfeeding | 2.7 L | 2.16 L | 73 | 8.6 | 9.1

 

The NHS keeps it simpler: aim for 6 to 8 cups or glasses of fluid a day, and it calls that “just a guide”. Water, lower-fat milk and lower-sugar drinks, including tea and coffee, all count.

## How the calculator works

Drinks a day = drinks from the guideline + exercise minutes ÷ 60 × sweat rate + hot hours × 0.3 L.

 
- The guideline amount is the adequate intake from the tables above. It covers a sedentary day in a mild climate.
 
- Exercise. Sweat you lose has to come back from drinks. The National Academies report lists measured sweat rates of about 0.7 to 1.0 L an hour for distance runners in temperate conditions, and 1.0 to more than 2.0 L an hour for competitive runners in the heat. I use 0.3 L for light activity, 0.7 L for moderate and 1.0 L for hard exercise or exercise in the heat. Sweat rates vary a lot between people, so the American College of Sports Medicine suggests finding your own: weigh yourself before and after exercise. Each kilogram you lose is about a litre of sweat.
 
- Heat. People working in desert heat sweated 0.3 to 1.2 L an hour in the studies the National Academies reviewed. I add the low end, 0.3 L an hour, for time spent working or on your feet outdoors in hot weather. Very active people who are always in hot weather often need 6 litres of total water a day or more.
 
- Glasses = litres from drinks ÷ your glass size. US fluid ounces = millilitres ÷ 29.57.

## When to ask a doctor

Needs vary with your body, your health and your day, and more is not always better. Talk to a doctor or nurse before changing how much you drink if:

 
- you have a kidney or heart condition, or you take water tablets (diuretics). With some kidney disease, the NHS says you may be told to reduce your fluids, including the water in soups and yogurt;
 
- you are pregnant or breastfeeding and unsure what applies to you;
 
- you are caring for an older person: thirst weakens with age, so the National Academies set older adults’ intake from younger adults’ figures;
 
- you have signs of dehydration that don’t go away, such as dark, strong-smelling pee, dizziness or unusual tiredness. The NHS lists when to get help on its dehydration page.

 

## FAQ

How much water should I drink a day?
For healthy adults on a sedentary day in a mild climate, the US National Academies’ adequate intake works out to about 2.2 litres from drinks for women and 3.0 litres for men. The European Food Safety Authority’s total water values are lower: 2.0 litres for women and 2.5 litres for men, food included. Exercise and heat add to both.

Is 8 glasses of water a day right?
It is a reasonable rule of thumb, but not an official one. The NHS suggests 6 to 8 cups or glasses of fluid a day as a guide, and the National Academies panel said it offers no rule of thumb based on glasses.

Do tea and coffee count toward my water?
Yes. The NHS counts tea and coffee, and the National Academies panel found no convincing evidence that caffeine leads to cumulative body water deficits, so caffeinated drinks count toward your total.

Does food count?
Yes. In the National Academies’ data, about 20% of total water came from food and about 80% from drinks. That’s why the drinks figure is lower than the total water figure.

Can you drink too much water?
Yes, but it is unusual. The National Academies panel noted that people occasionally drink amounts that can be life-threatening, while calling such cases highly unusual; it set no upper limit for water. Spread drinks through the day and ask a doctor if you have a condition that affects fluids.
